title: Take the tree count from the model when averaging cforest and aorsf trees
description:
The `cforest` and `aorsf` `tidypredict_combine_trees()` methods divided by `length(trees)` rather than by the model's tree count. That is the same number when a caller passes one element per tree, but orbital adds the trees in batches first so that no single generated expression exceeds a database's parser limits, and then passes one subtotal per batch. Those subtotals were averaged over the number of batches, which is wrong by a factor of the batch size.

Every other combiner sums rather than averages, so this was the only place the distinction mattered. The docs now state the contract explicitly, since it is what makes batching safe.

title: Document the extractor seam as a contract
description:
Phase 6 documentation, tidypredict side. Documentation only, no behavior change.

The three seam topics (`tidypredict_extractors`, `tidypredict_combine_trees`, `tidypredict_metadata`) were each written well for a caller holding one model, but none pointed at the others. Someone landing on `tidypredict_trees()` got no pointer to `tidypredict_combine_trees()`, which is exactly the trap the latter exists to prevent: the shape of the returned list invites summing, and summing is wrong for `blackboost` (offset and shrinkage), CatBoost (scale and bias), `aorsf` (NA guard) and every booster with an inverse link.

## What's added

**A coverage table** in `?tidypredict_extractors`, so a new backend is written against a spec rather than by imitation:

```
                 trees  class_trees  class_exprs  n_trees  combine
blackboost         x         .            .          x        x
C5.0               .         .            .          .        x
catboost.Model     x         .            .          x        x
cforest            x         .            .          x        x
earth              .         .            x          .        .
lgb.Booster        x         .            .          x        x
multnet            .         .            x          .        .
ObliqueForest      x         .            .          x        x
party              .         .            x          .        .
randomForest       x         x            .          x        x
ranger             x         x            .          x        x
rpart              .         .            x          .        .
xgb.Booster        x         .            .          x        x
```

Generated from the method tables rather than written by hand, and verified against them by a script: 13 classes checked, 0 mismatches.

**The rule the table reveals**, written up as an implementer section: `tidypredict_trees()`, `tidypredict_n_trees()` and `tidypredict_combine_trees()` are a set, implement all three or none. Per-tree expressions are not usable without a count to size them and a rule to recombine them. `C50::C5.0()` is the one deliberate exception, with a refusing `combine` method and no `trees` method, which the table makes visible as a single anomalous row rather than something you have to know.

Also documents `tidypredict_combine_trees(x, tidypredict_trees(x))` matching `tidypredict_fit(x)` as the check a new method should satisfy, since that catches a combination rule that was assumed rather than read out of the model.

**Cross-references** between all three topics, in all directions.

## Checks

- `devtools::test()`: FAIL 0 | WARN 6 | SKIP 1 | PASS 2707. The 6 warnings are pre-existing on `main`.
- `pkgdown::check_pkgdown()`: no problems.
- `devtools::document()` touches only the three intended `.Rd` files, no version churn.
- `air format .` clean.

title: Add tidypredict_combine_trees() and the last extractors
description:
T4 / phase 1d, and the last piece of the orbital new-backends plan's tidypredict-side work.

## The plan for this PR was wrong, in a way the code made obvious

Phase 1a claimed that **"any backend that gains a `tidypredict_trees()` method automatically gains `separate_trees` in orbital with no orbital change at all."** That only holds when a model combines its trees by a plain sum or mean. Checking the five backends this PR was supposed to cover, it holds for **one**:

| Backend | Trees? | How the model actually combines them |
|---|---|---|
| cforest | yes | plain mean ✓ |
| aorsf | yes | mean, inside a guard returning `NA` for a partial row ✗ |
| blackboost | yes | `offset + nu * sum(trees)` ✗ |
| C5.0 | yes | confidence-weighted vote over class labels, not summable ✗ |
| xrf | **none** | penalized glm on rule indicators, not an ensemble |

Adding the methods as specified would have let a caller drop blackboost's offset and shrinkage, and aorsf's missing-row guard: plausible wrong numbers rather than an error.

## `tidypredict_combine_trees(x, trees)`

Holds the combination rule alongside the trees. `trees` may be expressions **or symbols naming columns the trees were written to**, because computing each tree into its own column and then combining references to those columns is the case this exists for.

The rules, all of which a caller would otherwise have to know:

```
blackboost    offset + nu * sum(trees)
aorsf         mean(trees), inside an NA guard
catboost      scale * sum(trees) + bias, then an inverse link
xgboost       base_score + sum(trees), then the objective's inverse link
lightgbm      sum(trees), divided by n for boosting = "rf", then the link
randomForest  mean(trees), plus corr.bias rescaling when present
cforest       mean(trees)
```

**The identity is enforced structurally.** Every ensemble's `tidypredict_fit()` now routes through the two generics, so

    tidypredict_combine_trees(x, tidypredict_trees(x)) == tidypredict_fit(x)

holds by construction rather than by coincidence. The arithmetic was factored into one helper per backend (`rf_combine()`, `ranger_combine()`, `xgb_combine()`, `lgb_combine()`, `catboost_combine()`, `mboost_combine()`) called from both paths, so it cannot drift. Tests assert the identity **at the value level** for all nine backends, and again with `rlang::syms()` standing in for tree columns. It held on the first attempt for every backend, including DART and `binary:logistic`.

The xgboost helper is arranged so double-applying DART weights is structurally impossible: `assemble_xgb_formula()` is now `xgb_combine(apply_dart_weights(...))`.

## Two backends deliberately expose nothing

**Boosted C5.0** combines by a confidence-weighted vote where each trial contributes a class *label* plus a confidence, with `SelectClassGen()` breaking ties on that trial's own root class. There are no per-tree numbers, so splitting the trees apart is not an approximation of the model, it is a different model. `tidypredict_combine_trees()` refuses with an explanation rather than a bare "no method".

**xrf** is not a tree ensemble at all. It is a penalized linear model whose predictors are rule indicators, built as a `terms` list of coefficient times indicator, and it already works as a `pm_regression`. The plan listed it here on a false premise.

Multiclass lightgbm and catboost also refuse: their `tidypredict_trees()` output is a flat round-robin list whose adjacent trees belong to different classes, so it is not summable as a single ensemble.

## A comment of mine from #433 was wrong

`tidypredict_n_trees.lgb.Booster()` claimed single-leaf trees are dropped by the extractor. They are not: `lgb.model.dt.tree()` omits them but `add_lgb_stump_trees()` deliberately puts them back, because multiclass class assignment is positional and a gap shifts every later class (#419). Comment corrected.

## Verification

Suite `FAIL 0 | WARN 6 | SKIP 1 | PASS 2703`, up from 2675. `R CMD check` **with vignettes**: 0 errors, 0 warnings.

One thing worth flagging about the tests. The new ones initially passed under `devtools::test()` and failed under `R CMD check` with `could not find function "case_when"`. Tree expressions call `case_when()` unqualified, and `tests/testthat.R` attaches only testthat and tidypredict — they were passing only because an earlier test file had attached dplyr, which check does not reproduce. Fixed by evaluating against dplyr's namespace explicitly, so the tests no longer depend on run order.

Four pre-existing snapshots changed only in the reported call label, since the objective checks moved into the extracted helpers. Messages are byte-identical and the new labels are accurate.

## Noted, not fixed

- `apply_xgb_objective()` tests `base_score != 0` on a value `get_xgb_json_params()` can parse as length > 1, since its regex splits on commas. Unreachable today because multiclass objectives are rejected, but a latent trap.

title: Add generics describing what fitted expressions compute
description:
T2 / phase 1b of the orbital new-backends plan. `tidypredict_fit()` returns expressions but says nothing about what they mean, and **the meaning is not recoverable from their shape.** Two cases where guessing wrong is silent rather than loud:

- A `LiblineaR` logistic regression and a `LiblineaR` SVM classifier both return exactly one expression. Measured: the first lands in `[0.0066, 0.971]`, the second straddles zero at `[-2.25, 1.38]`. Thresholding the second at 0.5 as though it were a probability misclassifies every row whose value falls between 0 and 0.5.
- A multiclass probability list and a `quantreg::rq()` fit with several `tau` are both named lists of expressions of the same length. In the first, row sums are exactly 1; in the second they ran 31 to 84.

## The three generics

`tidypredict_output_type()`, `tidypredict_outcome_levels()`, `tidypredict_normalized()`. Documented at `?tidypredict_metadata`.

## Asked of the model, not attached to the result

Attributes on the fit result were the obvious design and do not work. Measured: on a named list, `x[lvl]`, `lapply()` and `unlist()` each drop them; on a language object a `deparse`/`parse` round trip drops them. orbital's own multiclass consumer does `class_eqs[lvl]` then `unlist()`, so the metadata would be gone before it could be read — in exactly the multiclass case that motivated it.

Independently, `tidypredict_save()` is `yaml::write_yaml()` on the parsed model, so attributes do not survive a round trip either, and it cannot accept a fit result at all (it tries to `parse_model()` a `call`).

Asking the model has nothing to strip, changes no existing return value, and matches the extractor-generic pattern from #433.

## Only four output types, and two surprises

There is **no `"logit"`**. Every multiclass list goes through one shared `expr_softmax()`, so values always already sum to one. `tidypredict_normalized()` is therefore always `TRUE` or `NA`, never `FALSE`. Kept anyway so callers can rely on the invariant instead of knowing it, and so a future non-normalizing backend can say so rather than silently break the assumption.

**`"class"` covers more than expected.** rpart, ctree, C5.0 and baguette bagger classification return a class *label* and no probability at all — there is nothing to argmax or normalize. And `xgboost`'s `binary:hinge` is also `"class"`: `apply_xgb_objective()` wraps it in `as.numeric(score >= 0)`, so it takes only the values 0 and 1. That makes using it as a numeric prediction wrong even though its type is numeric. I had it as `"numeric"` first and changed it after checking the values.

## Structure

44 `tidypredict_fit()` methods, but only **10** parsed-model types. So the `.default` methods route through `parse_model()` the way `tidypredict_fit.default()` does, and most methods sit on the `pm_*` classes. A backend gets a fitted-class method only where the parsed form is insufficient:

- rpart and party do not record their mode once parsed
- ksvm and glm do not record their response levels once parsed
- `parse_model.rqs()` returns a bare list rather than a `parsed_model`
- h2o has no `parse_model()` method
- LiblineaR needs its `type` to tell probability from decision value

Where mode or levels had to be detected, the existing signal is reused rather than a parallel one invented — `ksvm_is_classification()` is factored out of `parse_model_ksvm()`, and `bagger` reuses `bagger_classes()`.

## Verification

Suite `FAIL 0 | WARN 6 | SKIP 1 | PASS 2675`, up from 2537. The 6 warnings are pre-existing and in other files. `R CMD check` **with vignettes** gives 0 errors, 0 warnings (notes are a worktree `.git` and the pre-existing unstated `catboost`).

Every backend was checked by fitting a model and evaluating the returned expressions, not by reading source. For one representative of each output type the tests assert the *values*, not just the label: prob lists sum to 1, single probs stay in `[0,1]`, the `rqs` list demonstrably does not sum to 1, class models return labels drawn from their levels, and `binary:hinge` takes only the values 0 and 1.

One trap caught this way: `kernlab::lev()` returns the sorted response *values* for an SVR, so a naive implementation reported 25 numeric "levels" for a regression. Gated on `kernlab::type()`, with a test asserting `NULL`.

## Pre-existing issues noticed, not fixed here

- **`parse_model.rqs()` breaks the `parse_model()` contract**, returning a plain `list` of parsed models rather than a `parsed_model`. Anything routing through `parse_model()` generically cannot handle it, which is why `rqs` needs fitted-class methods.
- **`parse_model_lm()` calls `summary()` on `rq` fits**, which runs `rq.fit.br(ci = TRUE)` and warns "Solution may be nonunique" once per quantile. Parsing should not need the inference machinery; it makes `tidypredict_fit()` on an `rqs` noisy.

title: Replace the .extract_* functions with generics
description:
T1 / phase 1a of the orbital new-backends plan, and the highest-leverage change on either side: once a backend has a `tidypredict_trees()` method, orbital gets `separate_trees` support for it with no orbital change at all.

## The problem is worse than "ad-hoc"

I expected eight functions needing two generics. There are **eleven**, implementing **four** mutually incompatible contracts, and the `_classprob` suffix covers two of them:

| | Functions | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | xgb, lgb, catboost, rf, ranger `_trees` | flat list of per-tree expressions |
| **B** | rf, ranger `_classprob` | level-keyed list of per-tree expression lists |
| **C** | rpart, partykit `_classprob` | one whole-tree expression per level |
| **D** | earth, glmnet `_multiclass` | one **deparsed string** per level |

So two functions sharing the `_classprob` name return structurally different things, and two others return strings where everything else returns expressions.

## The generics

- `tidypredict_trees()` — A, 5 methods
- `tidypredict_class_trees()` — B, 2 methods
- `tidypredict_class_exprs()` — C and D, 4 methods
- `tidypredict_n_trees()` — 5 methods

Documented as one topic, `?tidypredict_extractors`, with each return shape stated explicitly rather than left to be inferred. `tidypredict_n_trees()` is new: consumers currently substitute for it by reading `$ntree`, `$num.trees`, `niter`, or `sum(startsWith(dump, "booster"))` off a raw model object, which orbital does in eleven places.

## Two deliberate behaviour changes

**earth and glmnet now return language objects**, not deparsed strings, so every extractor returns expressions.

**The partykit result is keyed by outcome level.** It was unnamed, which left callers assuming its position matched `levels()` of the outcome — orbital does exactly that. Worth noting rpart was *already* keyed, so only partykit changes; my first pass through the code suggested both were unnamed and that was wrong.

## Old names

Kept as thin wrappers. They are exported and each had an Rd, so an unknown caller is possible even though the Rd carried `\keyword{internal}`. The earth/glmnet wrappers deparse to preserve their return type and the partykit wrapper drops the new names, so all eleven behave exactly as before.

**`deprecate_soft()`, not `deprecate_warn()`.** orbital calls these from its own namespace in sixteen places, and warning there would show orbital users a message about a function they neither called nor can avoid. I verified this rather than trusting the semantics: a plain `library(orbital)` session emits **zero** warnings and still produces correct output, while orbital's own test run shows the warnings because testthat forces `lifecycle_verbosity`. A direct caller gets warned, which is who can act on it.

Adds `lifecycle` to Imports.

## Also worth knowing

`catboost`'s `niter` counts boosting **rounds**, not trees. For multiclass models they differ by the number of classes, so `tidypredict_n_trees.catboost.Model()` counts trees rather than trusting `niter`.

## Verification

Full suite `FAIL 0 | WARN 6 | SKIP 1 | PASS 2537`, up from 2469. The 6 warnings are pre-existing upstream fitting warnings (earth constant-y, glmnet small-class, nnet empty group). The new `test-deprec-extractors.R` covers all eleven wrappers: the deprecation signal, the preserved return shape, and the unchanged wrong-class error text.

Cross-checked against orbital: its suite passes on this build apart from one unrelated snapshot it deliberately has not accepted (the logit rewrite, which is waiting on a version bump).

Three things this shook out that I fixed rather than shipped: the rpart error was reporting against the generic's formal `x`, a name no user typed; `tidypredict_n_trees()` returned doubles for the two forest methods while promising an integer; and a `glmnet` class whose coefficients are all zero yields a bare numeric next to language siblings, so the documented contract now states that a constant may appear in place of an expression in any of these generics, and that element type is therefore not uniform within one result.

title: Fix cforest models under partykit 1.3-0
description:
`main` is currently red, and #433 inherited it. **The cause is partykit 1.3-0, released in the last day or so, not anything in either PR.**

## Evidence it is pre-existing

- `main` at 3bfa3c7 already fails: [run 32607353890](https://github.com/tidymodels/tidypredict/actions/runs/32607353890) reports `processing vignette 'partykit.Rmd' failed`.
- Checking out unmodified `main` locally and installing partykit 1.3-0 reproduces the identical error. With partykit 1.2.27 it passes.
- #432's own PR checks were green, and the failure appeared on the merge commit, which is the window the partykit release landed in.

## The bug

partykit 1.3-0 added a shim to its S3 methods that warns when a method is called directly instead of through the generic. It identifies the caller with:

```r
caller <- sys.call(-1)
if (is.null(caller) || as.name(as.list(caller)[[1L]]) != gfun) { ... }
```

`as.name()` errors on any call whose first element is not a symbol. **The generic's own frame is the method's caller**, so writing `partykit::gettree(...)` makes that first element the `::` call, and every cforest model dies with:

```
'language' object cannot be coerced to type 'symbol'
```

Note `is.null(caller) ||` short-circuits, which is why a bare top-level call looks fine and this only shows up from inside another function. It takes out `tidypredict_fit()`, `parse_model()`, and the partykit vignette, so `R CMD check` fails at vignette building rather than at tests.

Calling `partykit::gettree()` is correct usage, so this is an upstream regression. Worth reporting to partykit; this PR just unblocks us.

## The fix

Bind the generic to a local name and call it through that symbol.

The name has to be **`gettree`** specifically. The shim compares the symbol it recovers against the generic's own name, so `gettree` stays silent while any other name works but emits a spurious "calling partykit methods directly is deprecated" warning on every call. I verified both branches of that.

Only `gettree` is affected. I checked every partykit function tidypredict calls with a `::` prefix — `nodeids`, `nodeapply`, `as.party`, `id_node`, `is.terminal`, `kids_node` — and they are all fine.

## Verification

Under partykit 1.3-0: suite `FAIL 0 | WARN 6 | SKIP 1 | PASS 2475`, and `R CMD check` **with vignettes** gives 0 errors, 0 warnings. The remaining notes are a worktree `.git` and the pre-existing unstated `catboost` in vignettes.

The new test asserts both halves of the fix: no error, and no warning, so a future refactor that renames the binding gets caught rather than silently reintroducing warning noise.

Worth merging ahead of #433, which should then go green on rebase.

title: Give the unsupported-model error a condition class
description:
Groundwork for orbital consuming more tidypredict backends. Small, and it unblocks a fix on the orbital side.

## Problem

Errors reading "are not supported" cover two quite different situations:

- `abort_model_unsupported()`: **no method knows how to handle this model at all.**
- Everything else: the model class *is* handled, but this configuration of it is not. Multinomial `xrf` models, classification `dbarts` models, `randomForest` models fitted with `corr.bias = TRUE`, and about a dozen others.

A caller wrapping `tidypredict_fit()` needs to tell these apart. The first is a reason to fall back to another code path, or to report the model as unsupported in the caller's own vocabulary. The second is a genuine error that should propagate untouched.

orbital currently distinguishes them by matching message text, with `grepl("no applicable method for", ...)`. That worked against tidypredict 1.1.0 only because the failure surfaced as a raw dispatch error. Now that this case has a proper message, the match fails and orbital leaks a `tidypredict_fit()` error to a user who called `orbital()`. Matching on the new wording instead is not a fix: `"are not supported"` is far too broad, and it would silently relabel the configuration errors above as "this model class is unsupported", which is both wrong and confusing.

## Change

Add the condition class `tidypredict_unsupported_model` to `abort_model_unsupported()`.

Also route the duplicated copy of this message in `tidypredict_fit.default()` through that helper, so the two sites cannot drift. `call = rlang::current_env()` preserves the reported call exactly, which the snapshots confirm.

This is the first condition class in the package. Happy to rename it if you would prefer a different convention.

## Verification

Full suite: `FAIL 0 | WARN 6 | SKIP 1 | PASS 2469`. No error snapshot moved, which is the thing worth checking given the dedupe: the message and the reported call are both unchanged, only the class is added.

title: Support constant predictors in dbarts models (#363)
description:
Closes #363.

I went with option (a), actually supporting the case, because the fix turned out to be safe, local, and verifiable against `predict()`.

## What was going on

`bart_column_map()` walks the `drop` attribute of `model$fit$data@x` to map each column of the model matrix back onto a column of the data. That attribute has three shapes, and the old code only knew two of them:

- `FALSE`: a numeric predictor that was kept, one model matrix column.
- an integer vector of per-level counts: a factor, one column per retained level.
- `TRUE`: a predictor that `dbarts` dropped entirely because it is constant in the training data, and so has *no* column in the model matrix.

A `TRUE` entry fell into the factor branch, which looked for columns prefixed with `xconst.`. With the constant predictor last, the slice `cols[seq(length(res) + 1, length(cols))]` counted backwards and produced an `NA` element, `startsWith()` returned `NA` for it, and the `NA` subscript pushed a bogus entry into the map. The length check at the end then fired the internal "Unable to map the predictors" abort.

## The fix

Skip predictors whose `drop` entry is `TRUE`. They contribute no column, so the tree `var` indices, which index the retained columns, still line up; nothing else about the mapping changes. The factor-level slice is also rewritten as a positional mask so it can no longer run backwards.

A single-level factor is a related case that already worked by accident (its `drop` entry is a count vector, and no `f.z` column exists to match), and it is covered by the new test alongside the constant numeric.

## Verification

Exact agreement with `predict()` on the issue's reprex:

```
tidypredict_test(m, d)
#> All results are within the difference threshold
max(abs(colMeans(predict(m, d)) - <formula>))
#> 1.776357e-15
```

And on a larger fit mixing a constant numeric first, a real numeric, a multi-level factor, a single-level factor, and a second constant: max absolute difference `2.664535e-15`.

`devtools::test(filter = "bart")`: `[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 51 ]`.

title: Fix vignette errors: nonexistent function, wrong data, dead chunks
description:
Works through the checklist in #317.

## Broken code

- Five articles recommended `tidypredict_to_sql()`, which does not exist. They now say `tidypredict_sql(model, con)`, matching what the other articles already said. Same fix applied to the two articles that said `tidypredict_sql(model)` without a connection.
- `ranger.Rmd` and `rf.Rmd` suggested `mutate(iris, ...)` for a model fitted on `mtcars`.
- `glmnet.Rmd` printed `str(pm$trees[1])`, which is `NULL`. A glmnet parsed model has `terms`, not `trees`.
- `sql.Rmd` passed `path = ":memory:"` to `dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ...)`, where the argument is `dbname`, so an on-disk temp database was created instead.
- `sda.Rmd` called `sda::predict.sda()` directly rather than `predict()`.
- The empty "Works" columns in `C5.0.Rmd`, `rpart.Rmd`, `catboost.Rmd` and `h2o.Rmd` rendered as blank tables. Filled in, with the rows the other articles have; each mark was checked by running the function.

## catboost article

The setup chunk gated on `if (FALSE)`, and every chunk was a plain ```` ```r ```` block, so the whole article was dead code that CI never validated. The real `rlang::is_installed("catboost")` gate is back, the blocks are real chunks that degrade to `eval = FALSE` when catboost is missing, and the YAML title now matches the `\VignetteIndexEntry`. Verified by knitting with catboost installed.

## Coverage gap

`kernlab::ksvm()`, `mboost::blackboost()` and `xrf::xrf()` were supported but had no article. title: Make skip_if_no_h2o() skip cleanly instead of emitting 11 warnings
description:
Closes #316.

`h2o.init()` prints a cluster banner and reports both the "your cluster version is N old" advisory and a genuine cluster/package version mismatch as *warnings*. The old `skip_if_no_h2o()` used `suppressMessages()` plus `tryCatch(error = )`, which intercepts neither, so `devtools::test()` reported `WARN 11` instead of clean skips. It also treated a stale foreign cluster on `localhost:54321` as success and never shut the JVM down.

`tests/testthat/helper-h2o.R` now:

- calls `skip_on_cran()` and skips early when `Sys.which("java")` is empty;
- probes with `h2o.clusterIsUp()`, then `h2o.connect()`, and only falls back to `h2o.init()` if neither works;
- wraps the probe in `capture.output()` plus `withCallingHandlers(warning = \(w) invokeRestart("muffleWarning"))`;
- turns a version mismatch into a skip reason rather than success. The check is deliberately narrower than "any warning mentioning a version": the `h2o.init()` advisory that a cluster is older than the newest release fires for essentially every user and is harmless, so what is checked is that the running cluster's version equals `packageVersion("h2o")`. A `Version mismatch` warning is caught too;
- memoizes the probe so the cluster starts at most once per run, and registers `withr::defer(h2o.shutdown(prompt = FALSE), teardown_env())` when this helper is the one that started it.

The multiclass half of the issue (`preds[, domain]` vs H2O's `p`-prefixed probability columns) was already fixed on `main` by #360; `R/model-h2o.R` now selects those columns positionally, so it is left alone. No `NEWS.md` bullet: this is test infrastructure only.

`CONTRIBUTING.md` gains a short "Local setup for h2o and catboost" section explaining why a fresh checkout sees skips for those two backends.

### Verification

On a machine with `h2o` 3.44.0.3, `agua`, a JVM, and a live 3.44.0.3 cluster:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `devtools::test(filter = "h2o")` | `FAIL 0 \| WARN 11 \| SKIP 0 \| PASS 26` | `FAIL 0 \| WARN 0 \| SKIP 0 \| PASS 26` |

The h2o tests still all run and pass; the warnings are simply muffled. Re-running with `java` removed from `PATH` gives `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 11 | PASS 0`, so both the "h2o available" and "h2o unavailable" paths are exercised.

Full suite after the change: `FAIL 0 | WARN 6 | SKIP 1 | PASS 2475`. The 6 remaining warnings are unrelated to h2o (`quantreg`/`stats::summary.lm` "essentially perfect fit" and an `nnet::multinom` empty-group warning) and belong to other issues.

Not exercised locally: the version-mismatch skip branch and the "`h2o.init()` fails to start a cluster" branch, since this machine has a matching, working cluster. Those two are verified by reading only.

title: Test suite hardening: skip guards, cross-platform ranger tests, real assertions
description:
Three test suite issues, one commit each.

## Skip rather than fail without Suggests (#315)

Every `test_that()` block that reaches into a Suggests package now guards it with `skip_if_not_installed()`. Beyond the files the issue names this also covers the remaining `test-model-*.R` files, which had the same gap for `yaml`, `dbplyr`, `parsnip` and `DBI`. A script over the whole suite now reports zero unguarded blocks.

`parsnip:::predict.nullmodel()` is replaced by a plain `predict()` call; the S3 method is registered, so dispatch finds it.

Not done: the hard-dependencies-only CI job. Workflows are being changed in a separate PR, so that item is left open and this PR does not close it on its own account.

Closes #315

## Run the ranger tests on every platform (#312)

**What the platform-specific failure was.** `git log -L` points at 349e716, which introduced `expect_snapshot(rlang::expr_text(tf))` together with the 46 `skip_on_os()` calls. That snapshot embeds the split values `ranger` chose. `ranger` grows its trees with its own RNG, whose stream is not portable across compilers, so the snapshot could not hold on Windows or Linux and the blocks were guarded instead of fixed. It is the *only* platform-dependent assertion in the file: every other snapshot in `_snaps/model-ranger.md` is an error message, and everything else compares numerically against `predict()` on the machine running the test, which is portable by construction.

That snapshot is replaced by a structural check on the expression, and all 46 `skip_on_os()` calls are gone, along with the `skip_on_cran()` calls: none guards a slow fit, the largest forest in the file is five trees.

No guard is kept. I can only run macOS locally, so the Windows and Linux jobs on this PR are the actual verification; if one of them fails, the right response is to fix the assertion rather than restore the skip.

Also deletes the unused legacy extractors `get_child_info()`, `get_ra_path()`, `get_ra_tree()` and `get_ra_trees()` plus their tests. A repo-wide grep confirms nothing else called them and they were never exported, so there is no NEWS bullet.

`codecov.yml` patch coverage moves from `informational: true` with a 1% threshold to a real 90% target, so coverage can block a PR.

`NOT_CRAN=true devtools::test(filter = "ranger")`: `[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 91 ]`, down from 23 of 28 blocks skipping.

Closes #312

## Assert correctness rather than record it (#311)

Much of this issue has been fixed by the PRs that merged since it was filed, and I verified each claim against current `main` rather than acting on it:

- The `expect_snapshot(tidypredict_test(model))` idiom is gone. The only remaining `expect_snapshot(tidypredict_test(...))` calls all pass `error = TRUE`, which is a legitimate use. `tidypredict_test()` itself compares against `predict()` at a 1e-12 threshold, so the `expect_false(result$alert)` idiom now used throughout `test-model-xgboost.R` is a real correctness assertion.
- The bare `tempfile()` sites listed in the issue already use `withr::local_tempfile()`. The one survivor, `test-parsemodel.R:10`, is inside a snapshot of an error raised before anything is written.
- **The "configurations that never get tested" list is already covered**, exactly as the issue's follow-ups predicted. `test-model-catboost.R` loops `n_levels` over 2:8; `test-model-ksvm.R` has single-scaled-column tests for both regression and classification; `test-model-lightgbm.R` covers `missing_type` and `zero_as_missing`; `test-model-rf.R` and `test-model-ranger.R` both cover unordered, ordered, partition, awkwardly named, unused and missing factor levels. Nothing here fails, so **no live bug was found**. The bart `ntree = 200` case is being handled in a separate PR and is untouched here.

What this commit actually changes:

- `test-model-glmnet.R` proved only that `tidypredict_fit()` did not error for each family. It now compares against `predict()` at 1e-12.
- `test-model-glm.R` gains a direct `predict()` comparison across three formula shapes and five families.
- `round_print()` in `helper-printing.R` is **fixed, not deleted**: the issue says it has no callers, but it has around 30 and is documented in `CONTRIBUTING.md`. The `sub()` loop becomes a positional `regmatches<-`, so a short number cannot match inside a longer one, and the pattern now covers integers and scientific notation. The only snapshot this changes is xrf's, where `-7.154443e-5` becomes the canonical `-7.154443e-05`.
- The two round-trip tests that mutate `model$coefficients` before comparing are renamed so they are not mistaken for correctness tests.
- `generate-v3-fixtures.R` gives each fit its own seed.
- `test-backwards-compat-v3.R` tightens from 1e-6 to the 1e-12 suite standard. The xgboost fixture stays at 1e-7 with a comment: its leaf values are float32, and it fails at 1e-12 with a relative difference of about 2e-8.

Not done: converting the ~250 global `set.seed()` calls to `withr::local_seed()`. That is churn and is left open, so this PR does not close #311's parent concerns beyond what is listed above.

Closes #311

title: Select h2o multiclass probability columns positionally
description:
Fixes #360.

`tidypredict_test.H2OMultinomialModel()` built its comparison matrix with `preds[, domain, drop = FALSE]`, where `domain` is the outcome factor's levels. But `h2o.predict()` prefixes a probability column with `p` when the level is not a syntactic name, so an outcome with levels `"3"`, `"4"`, `"5"` returns `predict`, `p3`, `p4`, `p5` and the subset fails with `undefined columns selected`.

The probability columns follow `predict` in domain order, which the binomial method already relies on, so this selects them positionally the same way. `domain` is still passed to `test_results_multiclass()` for labelling.

`tidypredict_fit()` was never affected: the issue confirms the same model passes at 1.5e-09 once the levels are relabelled.

The new test in `tests/testthat/test-h2o.R` fits a GBM on `factor(mtcars$gear)`. Against `main` it fails with exactly the reported error; with the fix the full h2o file passes (`FAIL 0 | PASS 26`) against a live cluster.

title: Record why LightGBM stump trees must stay restored (#419)
description:
Comments only, no behavior change and no `NEWS.md` bullet.

#419 is already fixed by PR #407, which added `add_lgb_stump_trees()`. But #407's motivation was #401, the all-stump model that failed with "Model has no trees.", and the comment on the function records only that. The multiclass consequence is a separate property that happens to be carried by the same code, and it is the more likely one to be hit: it needs only one absent class, and it fails silently because the probabilities still sum to 1.

This moves that reasoning out of the issue and into the two places someone would be standing when they could undo it: the function itself, and the regression test.

The point being preserved is that restoring the dropped trees and keying off `tree_index` are two different fixes. #407 does the former. If a future change stops restoring them, the class assignment has to become index-aware instead, or the defect comes back unnoticed.

## Verification that #419 is closed

Confirmed on `main` rather than assumed, with a revert check. A 2-iteration, 3-class fit in which the third class is never observed; `lgb.model.dt.tree()` returns tree indices `0 1 3 4`, so the gap still occurs and the fix works by restoring the trees rather than by preventing it.

| | class 1 | class 2 | class 3 | max abs diff vs `predict()` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| before #407 (at `4bc6f91`) | 0.250363 | 0.150321 | 0.599316 | 0.599316 |
| current `main` | 0.798948 | 0.201052 | 0.000000 | 8.3e-17 |
| `predict()` | 0.798948 | 0.201052 | 0.000000 | |

The existing test `"a multiclass model with stump trees matches predict()"` covers this permanently: it asserts the tree-index gap is present and then compares elementwise against `predict()`, so it fails with the fix reverted.

`devtools::test(filter = "^model-lightgbm")`: 0 failures, 248 passing.

title: Make boosted C5.0 trials NA-aware
description:
Closes #416.

**Merge #421 first.** This branch is cut from `fix-417-c50-classprob` because it reuses `c50_na_cases()` and `c50_na_weight()` introduced there, but its base is `main` so it will not merge into a dead-end branch. If #421 merges first this reduces to the boosting commit alone.

## Verified mechanism

Read `src/classify.c` of the C50 source tarball (0.2.0) first, as the issue asked. The two questions it raised:

**Is the combination over class votes or over weighted distributions?** Over votes, one per trial. `PredictBoostClassify()`:

```
ForEach(t, 0, MaxTrial) {
  Best = PredictTreeClassify(Case, Pruned[t]);
  Vote[Best] += Confidence;
  Total += Confidence;
}
ForEach(c, 1, MaxClass) { ClassSum[c] = Vote[c] / Total; }
Best = SelectClassGen(Default, binfalse, ClassSum);
```

Only the winning class of each trial gets anything; the rest of that trial's distribution is discarded. Dividing by `Total` is a positive constant and cannot move the argmax, so it is dropped.

**Where does the per-trial confidence come from?** From `PredictTreeClassify()`, and it is reconstructible. That function picks `Best` as the argmax of the *raw* accumulated `ClassSum[c]`, starting from `DecisionTree->Leaf`, the trial's own root class, and replacing only on a strict `>`. It then rewrites `ClassSum[c]` as `(W * ClassSum[c] + prior[c]) / (W + 1)` with `prior` taken at that trial's root, and sets `Confidence = ClassSum[Best]`.

With no missing split value the case reaches exactly one leaf, so `Best` is that leaf's recorded class and `Confidence` is `(freq + prior) / (n + 1)`, the leaf confidence the existing expression already votes with (#287). A missing split value makes both the argmax and the confidence depend on the weighted descent, which is what was missing.

## The fix

- `parse_c50_trees()` now keeps each trial's root class, and each trial's `tree_info` carries it along with the outcome levels, so a trial can break its own ties the way `SelectClassGen()` does. As with #405 these are new fields, so a parsed model saved before this change falls back to the old expression.
- `c50_trial_na_votes()` builds one trial's vote for every class as `if_else(<class wins>, (W * S_c + prior_c) / (W + 1), 0)`, with `S_c` from `c50_na_score()` and `W` from `c50_na_cases()`, both in the linear `w * left + (1 - w) * right` shape.
- `c50_argmax_indicators()` states the "first score to attain the maximum" test directly (strict `>` against earlier classes, `>=` against later) rather than reusing `build_argmax_case_when()`, whose cascade would have cost a further factor of the class count.
- The whole thing sits behind the same guard #405 uses, so only rows actually missing a split value take it.

This is a fix, not an abort.

## Numeric verification

Sweep of 18 boosted models (6 seeds x 3, 5, 10 trials; 2 to 4 outcome classes; three continuous and two factor predictors), each scored on 400 rows with 15% `NA` in every predictor, against `C50::predict.C5.0()`.

| | mismatched rows |
| --- | --- |
| before | 1569 / 7200 |
| after | 0 / 7200 |

The new test fails on `main` and passes here, for both the fitted model and the `parse_model()` round trip.

## The cost, stated plainly

The weighted vote has to be stated once per class per trial, and each statement carries the tree recursion, so the formula grows linearly in trials and quadratically in outcome levels. Measured on one 600-row training set with four predictors:

| classes | trials | formula characters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 3 | 144k |
| 2 | 10 | 347k |
| 3 | 5 | 2.1M |
| 4 | 10 | 15.2M |

The worst case in the correctness sweep went from 547k characters to 20.5M, a factor of 37. Generation stays under a quarter of a second and evaluation is unaffected for rows with no missing value, but a boosted model with many outcome levels will produce a formula that is awkward to move around, and a SQL backend may well refuse it.

If that trade is not wanted, the alternative the issue sanctions is an informative abort for `trials > 1` with `NA`-containing new data. I went with the fix because the divergence it replaces is silent and the arithmetic is fully verified, but the abort is a one-function change from here and I am happy to swap it if you prefer.

I could halve the constant by writing the weighted combination as `right + w * (left - right)`, which states the weight once instead of twice, but that would also change the single-tree expression from #405 and #417, so I left it alone.

## Notes

Full suite: FAIL 0, one skip for h2o. No snapshot changes.

This is one of three PRs against `main` for the C5.0 follow-ups filed together (#417, #415, #416). Only this one has an ordering requirement (#421 first); all three touch `NEWS.md` and will conflict with each other in sequence.

title: Decode ranger partition splits from the packed split value (#414)
description:
Closes #414.

## Verified mechanism

Under `respect.unordered.factors = "partition"`, `ranger` does not order factor levels. It searches over subsets and stores the chosen subset packed into the bits of a single split value: bit `k - 1` is set when level `k` goes to the **right** child. Confirmed in `src/Tree.cpp` of ranger 0.18.0, `Tree::predictionTerminalNodeIDs()` lines 206-217, the branch taken when `isOrderedVariable(split_varID)` is `FALSE`:

```cpp
size_t factorID = floor(value) - 1;
size_t splitID = floor(split_values[nodeID]);
// Left if 0 found at position factorID
if (!(splitID & (1ULL << factorID))) { ... left ... } else { ... right ... }
```

The bit index is the level's position in `forest$covariate.levels` for that predictor, which is the factor's own level order (`predict.ranger()` reaches the C++ code via `data.matrix()`, so `value` is the level index).

The decode itself was already correct on `main` after #283, but it read the level set out of `ranger::treeInfo()`, which renders the mask for display. `R/treeInfo.R` lines 108-116 show that rendering only works up to 31 levels: above that `treeInfo()` warns "Unordered splitting levels can only be shown for up to 31 levels." and sets the whole `splitval` entry to `NA`. Parsing that `NA` as a comma-separated index list yielded `NA` as the left set, so `f %in% NA` was always `FALSE` and every row went right. `ranger` itself permits up to `.Machine$double.digits` = 53 levels (`R/ranger.R` lines 910-915), so 32 to 53 levels is a reachable, silently wrong region.

The fix reads the raw split value from `model$forest$split.values[[tree]]` and decodes the mask arithmetically (`bitwAnd()` is limited to 32 bits), covering the full 53 levels ranger allows. `treeInfo()`'s now-irrelevant warning about a column tidypredict no longer uses is muffled.

## Numerical evidence

Against `predict(model, df)$predictions`, elementwise, `splitrule = "extratrees"` (the only rule that makes many-level partition splitting tractable), 5 trees, `max.depth = 3`, 600 rows, one factor plus one numeric predictor. Max absolute difference:

| levels | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6 | 0 | 0 |
| 20 | 0 | 0 |
| 31 | 0 | 0 |
| 32 | 2.53 | 0 |
| 40 | 4.71 | 0 |
| 50 | 7.01 | 0 |

A wider sweep after the fix over 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 25, 35 and 50 levels x `max.depth` 2 and 5 x `respect.unordered.factors` of `"partition"`, `"order"` and `"ignore"`, through both `tidypredict_fit(model)` and `tidypredict_fit(parse_model(model))`, gives a max absolute difference of exactly 0 in all 96 comparisons. The new test fails on all four of its assertions with the decode reverted.

The sibling settings were checked as part of that sweep: `"order"` and `"ignore"` are correct at every level count tested, including above 31, since neither produces a bit-packed split value.

## Not verified

- Forests grown by ranger before 0.11.0, which store `forest$dependent.varID` and need `treeInfo()`'s `convert.pre.xy()` remapping. Split values are not remapped by that conversion, so reading them from the forest should be equivalent, but no such forest was built to check.
- Behavior when `newdata` carries factor levels that differ from the training levels. `ranger` re-codes only in `"order"` mode, so both `predict()` and the generated formula are on their own there; this is unchanged by this PR.

## orbital-facing

No abort was added and no behavior narrowed. `.extract_ranger_trees()` and `.extract_ranger_classprob()` both route through `build_nested_ranger_tree()` and so pick up the corrected decode; their output is unchanged for any model with 31 or fewer levels per unordered factor, and corrected above that. No signature or contract change for {orbital}.

title: Do not fire a C5.0 rule that tests a missing value
description:
Closes #415.

## Verified mechanism

Confirmed against `src/classify.c` of the C50 source tarball (0.2.0). The issue marked this partially verified; all three parts check out.

- `FindOutcome()` returns `-1` when the tested attribute is unknown.
- `Satisfies()` is `FindOutcome(Case, OneCond) == OneCond->TestValue`, and no `TestValue` is `-1`, so a condition on a missing attribute is false.
- `Matches()` requires every condition, so a rule testing a missing attribute never fires. The rule-tree route reaches the same place: `MarkActive()` only descends `Branch[v]` when `(v = FindOutcome(...)) > 0`.

The two things the issue asked to pin down:

- **What happens to the votes when a rule is skipped?** Nothing. `PredictRuleClassify()` only accumulates `ClassSum[R->Rhs] += R->Vote` over the rules in `Active[]`. A skipped rule is simply absent; there is no redistribution and no weighted descent as there is for a tree.
- **Is the default applied per rule or at rule-set level?** At rule-set level. `if (!TotWeight) return RS->SDefault` covers the no-rule-fires case, and otherwise `SelectClassGen(RS->SDefault, ...)` starts from the default and replaces only on a strict `>`, so it also wins ties.

Both were already what the generated argmax cascade does (default checked first with `>=`, every vote 0 when nothing fires). So the correct behaviour is expressible as-is, with no growth in the expression: the only thing wrong was that a condition against a missing value returned `NA` in R rather than `FALSE`, which poisoned the vote sum for that class and made the whole cascade fall through to the last class.

## The fix

Every column a rule tests is guarded with `!is.na()` in that rule's condition. This adds one term per distinct column per rule, so the expression stays linear.

This is a fix, not an abort.

## Numeric verification

Sweep of 20 rule-based models (10 seeds x `subset = FALSE`/`TRUE`, 2 to 4 outcome classes, three continuous and two factor predictors), each scored on 400 rows with 15% `NA` in every predictor, against `C50::predict.C5.0()`.

| | mismatched rows |
| --- | --- |
| before | 3218 / 8000 |
| after | 0 / 8000 |

The new test fails on `main` and passes here, for both the fitted model and the `parse_model()` round trip.

## Notes

One snapshot updated: the generated rule formula now carries the `!is.na()` guards.

Full suite: FAIL 0, one skip for h2o.

This is one of three PRs against `main` for the C5.0 follow-ups filed together (#417, #415, #416). They are not stacked, but all three touch `NEWS.md` and will conflict with each other in sequence; whichever merges first, the others need a `NEWS.md` rebase.

title: Document the ksvm matrix-interface name mangling (#418)
description:
Closes #418.

## Verified mechanism

Confirmed against kernlab's own source, `getMethod("ksvm", "matrix")`, which contains:

```r
if (is.null(y))
    x <- na.action(x)
else {
    df <- na.action(data.frame(y, x))
    y <- df[, 1]
    x <- as.matrix(df[, -1])
}
```

`data.frame()` defaults to `check.names = TRUE`, which is `make.names(..., unique = TRUE)`. The model matrix that `ksvm()` fits and stores therefore carries the mangled names, not the user's. kernlab never calls `make.names()` explicitly, so this one line is the whole source of the problem, the same line identified in #390 for the formula path.

## The names are not recoverable

Fitted a two-column matrix model with columns `a:b` and `c d` and printed every slot of the S4 object:

| slot | content |
| --- | --- |
| `xmatrix` | dimnames `a.b`, `c.d` (mangled) |
| `scaling$x.scale` | `scaled:center` / `scaled:scale`, named `a.b`, `c.d` (mangled) |
| `terms` | `NULL` on the matrix interface |
| `lev` | the response levels |
| `ymatrix`, `fitted`, `prior`, `prob.model`, `alpha`, `coef`, `alphaindex`, `SVindex`, `b`, `obj`, `nSV`, `error`, `cross`, `param`, `kpar`, `type`, `nclass` | numeric or response-side only, no predictor names |
| `kcall` | `.local(x = x, y = ..1, kernel = "vanilladot", prob.model = TRUE)`, names the promise but does not store the data |

No slot retains the original names.

## The mangling is also not detectable, so there is nothing to abort on

An earlier revision of this PR aborted when a stored column name contained a `.`. That was wrong and would have broken correct models. `make.names(unique = TRUE)` is the identity on names that are already syntactic and distinct, and everything it emits is syntactic and distinct, so **its image is contained in its fixed points**. Every name we could read back off a fitted model is therefore also a name a user could have passed in and had left untouched:

| original columns | stored as |
| --- | --- |
| `a:b`, `a.b` | `a.b.1`, `a.b` |
| `a.b.1`, `a.b` | `a.b.1`, `a.b` |
| `a`, `a` | `a`, `a.1` |
| `a`, `a.1` | `a`, `a.1` |
| `Sepal.Length`, `Petal.Width` | `Sepal.Length`, `Petal.Width` |

Each mangled case is byte-identical to an untouched case. Verified over 20,000 random column-name combinations that `make.names(make.names(x, unique = TRUE), unique = TRUE)` equals the inner result every time.

So a `.` is not evidence, and a `make.unique` suffix is not evidence either: `a, a.1` reaches the fitted object looking exactly like duplicated `a, a`. There is no signal at all, and any check here is a false abort on working code. `iris` through the matrix interface, about as ordinary as it gets, would have been rejected.

Given the choice between a silent wrong answer on non-syntactic columns and a loud false failure on the far more common dotted-but-correct columns, neither is acceptable as code, so this ships as documentation instead.

## What this PR does

- **No behavior change.** `parse_model.ksvm()` takes the stored matrix-interface names at face value, as before.
- A comment in `R/model-ksvm.R` records the fixed-point argument at the point where such a check would be added, so it does not get added back.
- `vignettes/models.Rmd` gains a "Support vector machines and non-syntactic names" section stating the limit and the two workarounds: give the matrix columns syntactic names, or use the formula interface, which does abort because it has a `terms` object to compare against.
- Regression tests so the false abort cannot return.

The #390 formula-interface abort is untouched.

## Honest scope: what is caught and what is not

**Caught:** non-syntactic *factor levels* on the formula interface, via the existing `ksvm_check_levels()` from #390. That path has a `terms` object, which is the extra information that makes detection possible.

**Knowingly let through:** a non-syntactic *column name* on the matrix interface, `ksvm(x, y)`. The generated formula will reference a column that does not exist, and the user sees an object-not-found error or `NA` at evaluation time rather than at parse time. This is a real defect and it stays open in effect, documented rather than fixed. It cannot be detected without also rejecting correct models, and it cannot be repaired because the original names are gone.

## Acceptance check

The iris matrix example now works and matches `kernlab::predict()`:

```r
x <- as.matrix(iris[1:100, c(1, 3, 4)])
m <- kernlab::ksvm(x, iris[1:100, 2], kernel = "vanilladot")
tidypredict_fit(m)
```

Max absolute difference against `kernlab::predict()` is 8.88e-16. Added as `matrix columns containing a dot match predict() (#418)`, together with an `a.b` / `a.b.1` pair (the shape a `make.unique` collision produces) and a plain syntactic case. All compare against `kernlab::predict()`, never against another tidypredict result.

`devtools::test(filter = "^model-ksvm")` passes, and the full suite is FAIL 0 with the usual single h2o skip.

title: Make C5.0 class probabilities NA-aware
description:
Closes #417.

## Verified mechanism

Confirmed against `src/classify.c` of the C50 source tarball (0.2.0), not taken from the issue text.

`PredictTreeClassify()` accumulates two things while descending: `ClassSum[c]`, the weighted class shares, and `ClassSum[0]`, the weighted leaf count (`Prob[0] += Fraction * T->Cases` in `FindLeafGen()`). It then reports

```
ClassSum[c] <- (ClassSum[0] * ClassSum[c] + Prior[c]) / (ClassSum[0] + 1)
```

with `Prior[c] = DecisionTree->ClassDist[c] / DecisionTree->Cases`, the class proportion at the root. So the `(W * S_c + prior_c) / (W + 1)` shape noted in passing in #405 is correct.

With no missing split value the case reaches exactly one leaf, `W` is that leaf's case count and `S_c` is `freq_c / W`, so the formula collapses to `(freq_c + prior_c) / (n + 1)`, which is what the generated nested `case_when()` already returns. Only a missing split value diverges, because `PredictFollowAllBranches()` descends every branch weighted by `Branch[v]->Cases / T->Cases` rather than falling through to `.default`.

## The fix

- `c50_na_cases()` writes out `W` with the same linear `w * left + (1 - w) * right` shape `c50_na_score()` already uses for `S_c`, so the expression stays linear in tree depth rather than exponential. The shared weight is factored out into `c50_na_weight()`.
- `c50_classprob_tree_info()` records `prob_class_index` and `prob_prior` on each per-class `tree_info`. As in #405 these are new fields, so a parsed model saved before this change falls back to the old expression rather than failing.
- `classprob_tree_expr()` wraps the ordinary nested `case_when()` in a guard so only rows actually missing a split value pay for the weighted descent. It is a no-op for the rpart trees that share the `baguette::bagger()` path.

## Numeric verification

Sweep of 15 C5.0 models (2 to 4 outcome classes, continuous and factor predictors), each scored on 400 rows of new data with 15% `NA` in every predictor, comparing every cell of the generated per-class expression against `predict(model, newdata, type = "prob")`.

| | mismatched cells (> 1e-6) |
| --- | --- |
| before | 6437 / 18000 |
| after | 0 / 18000 |

Largest remaining difference is 3.5e-08, which is C5.0's 32-bit float arithmetic. Largest difference before the fix was 0.749.

This is a fix, not an abort.

## Notes

Full suite: FAIL 0, one skip for h2o.

This is one of three PRs against `main` for the C5.0 follow-ups filed together (#417, #415, #416). They are not stacked, but all three touch `NEWS.md` and will conflict with each other in sequence; whichever merges first, the others need a `NEWS.md` rebase.

title: Reject an ordered predictor on the parsnip discriminant path (#393)
description:
This is a re-land of https://github.com/tidymodels/tidypredict/pull/406, which GitHub reports as merged but which never reached `main`. That PR was opened with `fix-391-colon-levels` as its base rather than `main`, and `fix-391-colon-levels` had already been merged to `main` separately via #403, so the stack was a dead end and the work was never on `main`. The commit is cherry-picked unchanged from the original branch, so the authorship and commit message survive. It applied to current `main` with no conflicts.

## The change

`sda`, `sparsediscrim` and `mixOmics` are all fit from a numeric matrix, so none of them can be handed an ordered factor directly, and none of them carries the contrast check the formula models do. parsnip builds the model matrix for the user, which is the one way `contr.poly` reaches these parsers, where its `.L` and `.Q` columns were read as level names and the predictions came out silently wrong by as much as 1.34.

The direct paths refuse the same fit, so this refuses it here too, with the same "the treatment contrast is the only one supported" error `MASS::lda()`, `MASS::qda()` and `mda::fda()` already give, rather than taking on `contr.poly` decomposition.

## Testing

Full suite on this branch: FAIL 0, PASS 2441, SKIP 8, against FAIL 0, PASS 2438, SKIP 11 on current `main`. The three previously skipped tests in `test-model-sda.R`, `test-model-sparsediscrim.R` and `test-model-mixOmics.R` now assert the error instead.

Closes #393

title: Fix the sparsediscrim collision and the mixOmics NA cases (#398)
description:
This is a re-land of https://github.com/tidymodels/tidypredict/pull/408, which GitHub reports as merged but which never reached `main`. That PR was opened on top of #406, which was itself based on `fix-391-colon-levels` rather than `main`; `fix-391-colon-levels` had already been merged to `main` separately via #403, so the whole stack was a dead end and neither PR's content is on `main`. The commit is cherry-picked unchanged from the original branch, so the authorship and commit message survive.

This one targets `main` directly and does **not** depend on #393's code. The cherry-pick conflicted only in `NEWS.md` and `tests/testthat/_snaps/model-sparsediscrim.md`, where the original commit carried along the neighbouring #393 bullet and snapshot; those were dropped here and belong to the re-land of #393 in the companion PR. No behaviour was changed in resolving the conflicts. The two PRs can be merged in either order.

## The changes

Three separate sub-items:

**(a) sparsediscrim, colliding model matrix column.** `parse_model()` and `tidypredict_fit()` now reject a fit whose model matrix has two columns with the same name, which happens when a factor level and another predictor expand into the same name, such as level `y2` of `g` against a predictor `gy2`. `sparsediscrim::predict()` reselects those columns out by name and so silently uses one of them twice, disagreeing with the fit it came from by as much as 0.84, and errors outright on a parsnip fit. There is no answer that matches both.

**(b) mixOmics, constant predictor.** A predictor that never varied, which is what an unused factor level expands into, has a scale of zero and so a `NaN` coefficient. That made the fit fail with "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" from the `coef == 0` test that drops zero terms. `predict()` zeroes such a column, so the coefficient is zeroed too.

**(c) mixOmics, missing values in new data.** `predict.mixo_pls()` centers and scales `newdata` and then does `x[is.na(x)] <- 0`, i.e. it fills each missing predictor in at its training mean rather than propagating the `NA`. This records that value on the field so the generated formula does the same.

### A note on sub-item (c)

Fixing (c) makes every mixOmics formula noticeably longer, because each predictor becomes `ifelse(is.na(disp), 230.7219, disp)`. That is the price of agreeing with `predict.mixo_pls()`. It changes the `returns the right output` snapshot, which is the whole of the `_snaps/model-mixOmics.md` diff here.

**Sub-item (c) can be dropped on its own** if you would rather mixOmics keep propagating `NA` and keep the shorter formulas. It is independent of (a) and (b). Say the word and I will strip it out.

## Testing

Full suite on this branch: FAIL 0, PASS 2441, SKIP 8, against FAIL 0, PASS 2438, SKIP 11 on current `main`. Three previously skipped tests across `test-model-sparsediscrim.R` and `test-model-mixOmics.R` now run.

Closes #398

title: Respect corr.bias and fuzzyThreshold in ensemble parsers
description:
Closes #395.

Two options that change `predict()` output and that the parser never read. One is supported, the other is refused; both are the same shape of bug.

## `randomForest(corr.bias = TRUE)`: implemented

`predict.randomForest()` ends with `yhat[keep] <- object$coefs[1] + object$coefs[2] * yhat[keep]`, where `coefs` is the intercept and slope of a regression of the observed values on the out-of-bag predictions, kept on the fit only when `corr.bias = TRUE`. That is a plain affine rescale of the forest average, everything it needs is on the model, and it is exactly reproducible, so it is implemented rather than refused. It is applied to the mean inside the existing incomplete-row guard, so a row with a missing predictor still comes back `NA`, as `predict()` returns for it.

`.extract_rf_trees()`, which {orbital} calls, returns the individual tree expressions and has no place to put a correction of their average, so it now aborts for such a model instead of returning trees that quietly average to the wrong thing.

Numerically, for `mpg ~ wt + hp + disp` on `mtcars` with `ntree = 20`: max abs difference against `predict()` is 0 with the fix and 0.2103 without it, matching the 0.21 reported in the issue. The parsed path is asserted too.

## baguette C5.0 `fuzzyThreshold = TRUE`: abort

A soft threshold sends a case near the split point partly down both branches, weighted by where it falls between the `low` and `high` bounds C5.0 records. That is not expressible as a hard `<=` comparison, and `tidypredict` already refuses it for a single `C50::C5.0()` fit. The bagged case was not refused because `c50_check_supported()` reads `model$control$fuzzyThreshold` and {baguette} runs its base fits through `butcher()`, which empties `control`. The option is now detected from the tree text instead, where C5.0 writes `low=` and `high=` beside the `cut` of a soft split and writes neither for a hard one. That fixes the bagged case and any other butchered C5.0 fit, and reuses the existing error message.

Aborting rather than implementing keeps the bagged case consistent with the single-tree case, which chose abort for the same reason.

## Testing

Both `skip()` calls added by #392 are removed. Baseline on `origin/main`: FAIL 0, SKIP 11, PASS 2438. After: FAIL 0, SKIP 9, PASS 2442.

One PR rather than two: the halves resolve differently but the diff is small and the issue tracks them as one item.

Note: `R/model-C5.0.R` is touched, by two lines plus a helper, because that is where the fuzzy-threshold check lives.

title: Follow ranger's learned missing-value direction
description:
Closes #394

## Verified mechanism

Since ranger 0.17.0 the default `na.action = "na.learn"` handles `NA` in the training data internally. Per `?ranger` and `src/Tree.cpp`, at each node where a missing value was seen during growing, ranger picks a direction (left or right) by split criterion and saves it as that node's default direction.

`Tree::predict()` (`src/Tree.cpp`, lines ~186-218) consults it only for **ordered or numeric** splits:

```cpp
if (prediction_data->isOrderedVariable(split_varID)) {
  if (any_na && std::isnan(value)) {
    if (child_nodeIDs.size() >= 3 && child_nodeIDs[2][nodeID] > 0) {
      nodeID = child_nodeIDs[2][nodeID];   // learned default child
    } else {
      nodeID = child_nodeIDs[0][nodeID];   // otherwise left
    }
  } ...
```

An unordered ("partition") split takes the bitmask branch and never looks at the default direction, so its existing level-collapsing handling is untouched.

The issue stated the mechanism correctly ("ranger routes NA per node"). It speculated the metadata might be missing from the convenient accessor, as with LightGBM; it is. `ranger::treeInfo()` exposes only `leftChild`/`rightChild`, but `model$forest$child.nodeIDs[[tree]]` gains a **third** vector when the model learned any directions. An entry of `0` means "nothing learned, go left".

This is *not* the C5.0 shape: ranger picks one side, it does not descend both and combine, so no weighted-sum expression is needed and the formula does not grow.

## Fix

`ranger_missing_right()` reads the third child vector and marks the nodes whose learned default is the right child. `ranger_split_condition()` then omits the `is.na(x) |` term for those nodes, which lets `case_when()`'s `.default` carry the row right. Everything else is byte for byte identical, so NA-free models and NA-free rows are unaffected. The flag rides on the split info, so both the live `tidypredict_fit()` path and the v3 parsed-model path are covered; a parsed model saved before this change has no such field and falls back to the old behavior.

One line in the shared `R/tree-nested.R` guards the `missing = "left"` branch on the new field. `missing = "left"` is used by ranger only, and the guard is inert when the field is absent.

## Numerical evidence

Compared against `predict.ranger()$predictions`, both the live formula and the parsed-model path:

| configuration | max abs diff (before) | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| mtcars, NA in `wt` | 1.48 | 0 |
| mtcars, NA in `wt`/`hp`/`disp`, depths 2/4/10 | up to 3.1 | 0 |
| iris plus `Species` factor, NA in two numerics | 0.014 | 0 |
| 60-config sweep (12 seeds x 5 depths, NA in 3 predictors) | - | 0 |
| mtcars, no NA in training | 0 | 0 |

Revert check: keeping the new tests and reverting `R/model-ranger.R` plus `R/tree-nested.R` gives **8 failures**; with the fix, 0.

## Test counts

- `origin/main` baseline: FAIL 0 | SKIP 11 | PASS 2438
- this branch: FAIL 0 | SKIP 10 | PASS 2446

The removed `skip()` is the one in `test-model-ranger.R` titled "a forest trained on data containing NA matches predict()".

## Separate issue

`respect.unordered.factors = "partition"` disagrees with `predict()` by up to 0.038 **even with no NA anywhere in training or prediction**, on rows that contain no missing value. That is an unrelated pre-existing bug in the unordered bitmask split handling, out of scope here, and should get its own issue.

title: Map xrf dummy columns against the model matrix
description:
Closes #396.

## Mechanism

Confirmed as stated in the issue, with one clarification. `xrf_feature_field()` checked `feature %in% vars` before matching factor levels, so with a factor `cyl` (levels 4/6/8) and a separate column literally named `cyl4`, the `cyl4` dummy of `cyl` was resolved as the raw `cyl4` column. The generated formula then contained `cyl4 * 1.6156`, which warns (`'*' not meaningful for factors`) and evaluates to all `NA`. Reordering the two string checks would not be a general cure: the collision is between a dummy name and a raw name, and either order guesses.

## Fix

The raw names are recoverable. `model$glm$formula` is a full `terms` object for the rule-augmented formula and `model$glm$xlev` records every factor's levels, so the model matrix `xrf` fit on can be rebuilt from a synthetic frame and its `assign` attribute read. `xrf_feature_map()` does that once per parse and returns a name-to-column map, which `xrf_feature_field()` now consults first; the old string matching remains only as a fallback for a fit whose model matrix cannot be rebuilt. This is the `term_fields()` approach from #374/#377 applied to xrf's own resolver. Two model matrix columns sharing a name is genuinely ambiguous, and now aborts informatively rather than guessing.

This is a visible-failure bug, not a silent-wrongness one: the affected fit warns and returns `NA`.

## Testing

The pre-existing `skip()` in `tests/testthat/test-model-xrf.R` ("a variable named like another variable's dummy column is mapped correctly") is removed and now passes, checked numerically against `predict.xrf(sparse = FALSE)`. With the fix reverted it fails with all-`NA` actuals. There was one other xrf skip in that file, about factor-level naming; it is the same issue and is the one resolved here.

Full suite: FAIL 0. Baseline on `origin/main` was PASS 2438 / SKIP 11; this branch alone moves one skip to a pass.

title: Rebuild LightGBM stump trees from the JSON dump
description:
Closes #401.

## The problem

When LightGBM cannot make a single split it halts boosting after one iteration and emits a tree that is a bare leaf. `lightgbm::lgb.model.dt.tree()` reports **no rows at all** for such a tree, so `parse_model()` produced `trees = list()` and `tidypredict_fit()` aborted with `"Model has no trees."`, while LightGBM's own `predict()` returned the constant for every row.

I confirmed the mechanism before writing anything. For the issue's reproducer `m$current_iter()` is 1, `nrow(lgb.model.dt.tree(m))` is 0, and the JSON dump carries the value in full:

```
$ :List of 5
  ..$ tree_index    : int 0
  ..$ num_leaves    : int 1
  ..$ tree_structure:List of 2
  .. ..$ leaf_value: int 5
  .. ..$ leaf_count: int 50
```

A stump tree's `tree_structure` is exactly a `leaf_value`/`leaf_count` pair with no `split_index`, which is what the fix keys on.

## A second, silent bug

The dropped tree does not have to be the only one. In a multiclass model the trees of a class with no representation in the data are stumps while the other classes split normally, so `lgb.model.dt.tree()` returns tree indices `0 1 3 4` for a 2-iteration, 3-class fit. tidypredict then had four trees for three classes and assigned them to classes by position, which produced *wrong predictions with no error*:

```
        class_0   class_1   class_2
before  0.2355    0.2390    0.5255
predict 0.5473    0.4527    9.96e-16
```

That case now matches `predict()` exactly.

## The fix

`add_lgb_stump_trees()` walks `dump$tree_info`, finds each tree whose `tree_structure` has no `split_index`, and rebuilds it as the single leaf row the rest of the parser already knows how to handle (`get_lgb_tree()` and `build_nested_lgb_tree()` both have a stump branch). Rows are re-sorted by `tree_index`, so tree order, and with it the multiclass assignment, is restored. It is called from both `get_lgb_trees()` (parsed path) and `extract_lgb_trees_nested()` (fitted path), right after `add_lgb_missing_type()`. A model with no stumps returns from the filter immediately and is untouched.

## Verified numerically, not structurally

Every check compares against LightGBM's own `predict()`, on all three configurations the issue lists plus multiclass:

| Configuration | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Constant outcome, `nrounds = 3` | matches `predict()`, 50 rows |
| Same model saved and reloaded through YAML (parsed path) | matches `predict()` |
| Single training row | matches `predict()` |
| bonsai `boost_tree(trees = 5, tree_depth = 3, min_n = 1)` on a lone 4-level factor | matches `predict()` |
| Multiclass, every tree a stump | matches `predict()` for all 3 classes |
| Multiclass, only some trees stumps | matches `predict()`; was silently wrong before |

## Dependency on #402

Once the model parses, it hits #397's problem too: the formula is a bare constant, `rlang::eval_tidy()` has nothing to recycle against, and it returns a length-1 scalar. The fix is #402's `expr_recycle_over_column()`, applied here to both the single-output and the per-class multiclass returns of `assemble_lgb_formula()`.

**#402 is not merged**, so this branch carries a copy of `expr_recycle_over_column()` in `R/misc.R`, byte-identical to the one in #402 including its comment. This is flagged rather than silent: **whichever of the two PRs merges second should drop its own copy of the helper when rebasing.** Only the helper is duplicated; #402's call sites (ranger, xgboost, bagger, xrf) are not touched here, and this PR's only other change to a shared file is that one addition to `R/misc.R`.

## Tests

The old test *"single leaf tree (stump) has empty path"* was vacuous: it hand-built a `tree_df` holding one leaf row, a shape real `lgb.model.dt.tree()` never returns for a stump model, since it returns nothing. It is replaced by five tests built from real fitted models, one per row of the table above, each comparing against `predict()`.

Suite goes from `FAIL 0 | SKIP 19 | PASS 2374` to `FAIL 0 | SKIP 19 | PASS 2379`, measured on a clean `origin/main` worktree and on this branch.

## orbital compatibility

**orbital is unaffected, and slightly better off.** `.extract_lgb_trees()` now returns stump trees it previously omitted, which is exactly the case `orbital/R/model-lightgbm.R:76` works around: `lightgbm_multiclass()` compares `length(trees)` against `niter * num_class` and reconstructs the tree indices from the dump when they disagree. With this change they agree, so it takes the simple branch and gets the same, correct class assignment; the workaround branch becomes dead but stays harmless. `parse_model()`'s output shape is unchanged, only the number of trees in it.

Verified by installing this branch into a separate library and running orbital's LightGBM suite against it: `model-lightgbm` passes 43/43.

title: Reject an ordered predictor on the parsnip discriminant path
description:
Closes #393

Stacked on #403 (#391). Review only the second commit; base retargets to `main` once #403 merges.

## Decision: abort, not support

**Aborting.** `contr.poly` decomposition was judged not worth supporting on the direct path (#343), and `MASS::lda()`, `MASS::qda()` and `mda::fda()` all refuse the same fit today. Supporting it here would mean these three engines accept through parsnip what four other models reject, and would commit the parsers to reading `.L`/`.Q` loadings, which no other part of the package does. The user-visible answer is one error message shared by every model.

## Verified mechanism (the issue's framing is not quite right)

The issue says the parsnip path "routes around" the guard. It does not: there is no guard on these paths to route around. `sda()`, `sparsediscrim` and `mixOmics` are all fit from a numeric matrix and so have no formula for `acceptable_formula()` to check, and `parse_model.model_fit()` dispatches straight to `parse_model_sda()` / `parse_model_sparsediscrim()` / `parse_model_mixomics()`. It is a different code path that predates the guard, the second of the issue's two hypotheses. Reproduced at 0.79 for `sda`, and `m$preproc$terms` carries `dataClasses` of `"ordered"` for the predictor, which is all the check needs.

## Fix

`acceptable_preproc()` in `R/tidymodels.R` applies the existing `acceptable_ordered()` to `model$preproc$terms`, called from `parse_model.model_fit()` and from the mixOmics branch of `tidypredict_fit.model_fit()` (which bypasses `parse_model.model_fit()`).

The check deliberately lives in the parsnip dispatch and **not** in `preproc_fields()`. I tried `preproc_fields()` first and it broke a passing test: a `sparsediscrim` formula fit supplies a `preproc` of its own built from `model$.terms`, and its expansion names every column after a level (`fp`, `fq`, `fr`) whether the factor is ordered or not, so that fit is correct today and must keep working. Only parsnip's model matrix uses `contr.poly`.

`term_fields()` in `R/model-lm.R` was **not** touched.

## Tests

The three `skip()`s from #388 (`test-model-sda.R`, `test-model-sparsediscrim.R`, `test-model-mixOmics.R`) are replaced with snapshot tests asserting the abort and its message. The existing `sparsediscrim` formula-interface ordered-factor test, which compares numerically against `predict()`, still passes unchanged.

Full suite: FAIL 0, PASS 2376 -> 2379, SKIP 17 -> 14.

title: Fix the sparsediscrim collision and the mixOmics NA cases
description:
Closes #398

Stacked on #406 (#393), which is stacked on #403 (#391). Review only the third commit; base retargets as the stack merges.

## (a) sparsediscrim label collision: **rejected, not fixed**

The issue frames this as the #376 label-collision class. It is not. `parse_model_sparsediscrim()` already decomposes the labels correctly here: I confirmed the parsed model puts `g == "y2"` on coefficient 2 and the ordinary column `gy2` on coefficient 4, which is what the fit means.

The 0.84 difference comes from `sparsediscrim` itself. `lda_diag.formula()` fits on the real model matrix, whose columns are `gx1`, `gy2`, `gz3`, `gy2` (`col_names` genuinely holds a duplicate, and the two `xbar` entries differ: 0.364 vs 0.481). `predict.lda_diag()` then rebuilds the matrix and does `x[, object$col_names]`, which returns the *first* `gy2` for both entries, so `predict()` never sees the predictor at all and contradicts the fit it came from. Through parsnip it is worse: the matrix is made unique to `gy2.1`, a name no new data has, and `predict()` fails with "undefined columns selected".

There is no output that matches both the fit and `predict()`, and matching `predict()` would mean baking an upstream bug into generated SQL. Consistent with the abort decision in #393, `tidypredict_fit()` now refuses the fit and says which column collided and what to do about it. The `skip()` becomes a snapshot test of that abort.

## (b) mixOmics unused factor level: fixed

An unused level expands into a constant column, whose `scaled:scale` is 0, so `b_hat / scale_x` is `Inf`/`NaN` and the intercept becomes `NaN` too; `build_terms(drop_zero = ...)`'s `coef == 0` test then failed with "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed". `predict()` rescales the same column to `NaN` and then zeroes it along with any other missing value, so it contributes nothing. `mixomics_coefs()` now sets a zero-scale column's coefficient to 0 before folding the intercept, which is exactly what `predict()` does.

## (c) mixOmics newdata containing NA: fixed

Verified in `predict.mixo_pls()`: after centering and scaling `newdata`, it does `x[is.na(x)] <- 0`, which is filling each missing predictor in at its training mean rather than propagating the `NA`. `mixomics_coefs()` now returns the training centers and `mixomics_impute()` records the relevant one on each single-column field, so the formula emits `ifelse(is.na(disp), 230.7219, disp)`. Interaction terms are left alone, since the mean of a product is not the product of the means.

**Note for review:** this makes every mixOmics formula noticeably longer, and the `returns the right output` snapshot changes accordingly. That is the visible cost of agreeing with `predict()`; it is called out in `NEWS.md`.

## R/model-lm.R

`term_fields()` was **not** touched. `lm_constructor()` gained one strictly additive branch: if a field carries an `na_val`, its expression is wrapped in `ifelse(is.na(col), na_val, ...)`. No existing model sets `na_val`, so every other model's output is byte-identical, which the full suite confirms.

## Tests

The three `skip()`s from #388 are gone: (a) becomes a snapshot test of the abort, (b) and (c) become numeric comparisons against `mixOmics::predict()`.

Full suite: FAIL 0, PASS 2379 -> 2382, SKIP 14 -> 11.

title: Return one prediction per row for all-stump models
