Closes #305

title: Keep rank-deficient lm and glm fits predictable
description:
Ticks **only the first box** of #308. Items 2 (label parsing) and 3 (prediction intervals and case weights) are untouched and stay open.

## The problem

`parse_model_lm()` called `qr.solve(qr.R(model$qr))` on every parse. A rank-deficient fit has a singular R factor, so the parse aborted for a model whose fitted values are well defined, even though `tidypredict_fit()` never touches the QR decomposition.

The issue understates the reach: two everyday shapes fail, not one.

```r
set.seed(1); n <- 120
d <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = runif(n, 0, 10))
d$y <- 2 * d$x1 - 0.5 * d$x2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)

tidypredict_fit(lm(y ~ x1 + xdup, transform(d, xdup = d$x1)))    # duplicated column
tidypredict_fit(lm(y ~ x1 + xconst, transform(d, xconst = 1)))   # zero-variance predictor
#> Error: Unable to calculate inverse of QR decomposition.
```

A predictor with no variance is not mentioned in the issue and is the more realistic way to hit this. Both fail identically for `glm()`, gaussian and binomial. `predict()` handles all of them.

## The fix

Drop the `NA` coefficients R leaves for the terms it could not identify, as `predict()` does, and build the inverse from the leading `rank` rows and columns of the R factor: exactly the columns whose coefficients survive. That block is not singular, so prediction intervals keep working for rank-deficient models as well, which was better than expected.

The QR failure no longer aborts the parse. `qr_inverse_lm()` returns `NULL` when no inverse can be formed and `te_interval_lm()` reports it with a cli message, which is the only place the QR is required. Previously that path failed with ``Must supply `.init` when `.x` is empty``. This also removes the `grepl("singular matrix", cnd$message)` test on an untranslated English message and the bare `stop(cnd)` re-raise, both noted as secondary in the issue.

## Measured

Max absolute difference against the modelling package's own `predict()`, 120 rows:

| model | shape | fit | interval |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lm` | duplicated column | 8.9e-16 | 8.9e-16 |
| `lm` | zero-variance predictor | 8.9e-16 | 8.9e-16 |
| `lm` | `mpg ~ cyl_f * gear_f`, 1 aliased coef | 0 | n/a |
| `glm` gaussian | duplicated column | 8.9e-16 | n/a |
| `glm` binomial | zero-variance predictor | 1.1e-16 | n/a |
| `lm` full rank (regression check) | `mpg ~ wt + disp` | 3.6e-15 | 0 |

Intervals compared against `predict(interval = "prediction")[, "upr"]`.

## Other classes checked

`parse_model_lm()` is shared by `lm`, `glm` and `rq`. `quantreg::rq()` refuses to fit a singular design itself and stores no `$qr`, so it takes the same `NULL` path as before: unchanged. The parsnip `linear_reg()` `lm` and `glm` engines route through the same parser and now work on rank-deficient fits (4.4e-16 against `predict()`). The other callers of `build_terms()` (`lda`, `qda`, `fda`, `sda`, `sparsediscrim`, `mixOmics`, `multinom`, `glmnet`) pass `qr = NULL` and were not touched.

## Tests

New tests in `tests/testthat/test-model-lm.R` for both shapes, for `lm` and `glm`, compared against `stats::predict()`. Each was confirmed to fail before the fix (4 failures on the reverted source). The old `#124` snapshot test asserted the abort that this PR removes, so it now asserts the fitted values match `predict()` instead.

`devtools::test()`: `FAIL 0 | WARN 13 | SKIP 0 | PASS 2002` (the warnings are the stale local H2O cluster). `devtools::check()` is clean apart from a hidden-directory NOTE from the worktree and one H2O REST failure in `test-h2o.R:142`, both unrelated to this change.

title: Build a stump tree without a case_when()
description:
Ticks the three main boxes of #310.

- [x] **`generate_case_when_tree()` crashes on a root-only tree.** `generate_tree_node()` returns a bare prediction for an empty path, and `rlang::f_rhs()` on it aborts with `` `x` must be a formula ``. A stump is now returned as its constant prediction. The guard tests the node's path rather than whether the built node is a formula, because in `mode = "ifelse"` a perfectly ordinary single-condition node is also not a formula.
- [x] **`.build_case_when_tree()` emits invalid code for a non-numeric stump.** The `is.numeric()` guard let a classification stump through to `case_when(.default = "a")`, which dplyr rejects with `` `...` can't be empty ``. It now guards on the absence of a condition, so the contract this function has with {orbital} is unchanged for every tree that already worked.
- [x] **`parsedmodel$general$mode` relies on `$` partial matching.** Now `general[["mode"]] %||% ""`.

Left out, as the issue says is fine: all six lower-priority items at the bottom of #310 (`path_formulas()` and `type = "all"`, the single-element non-intercept prediction, the `tree-nested.R` dangling-child and `is_categorical` cases, `build_nested_from_paths_recursive()` trusting `leaves[[1]]`, and the never-`FALSE` `default` argument).

## On how box 1 is reached

The issue says the crash is reachable for any saved v1/v2 ranger or randomForest parsed model containing a stump, and that `ranger(y ~ x, d)` on a constant `y` produces one. Half of that holds.

`ranger::ranger()` does produce a one-row `treeInfo()` on a constant outcome, and feeding a v2 parsed model with such a tree to `tidypredict_fit()` does crash exactly as described. But no released tidypredict could ever have written that parsed model: `parse_model()` in 0.5.1 and in 1.0.1 both abort on a ranger stump before `$trees` is built (`Can't recycle `.x` (size 0)` and `attempt to select less than one element in integerOneIndex` respectively), and 1.0.1's `parse_model.randomForest()` aborts on a randomForest stump too. So the practical route in is a v1/v2 parsed model that was edited, hand-written, or produced by something other than a released `parse_model()` and then read back with `as_parsed_model()`. Box 2 is the one that is reachable today through a supported entry point, since {orbital} calls `.build_case_when_tree()` directly with class-label predictions.

Box 3 is invisible to users on its own, so it gets no `NEWS.md` bullet; the other two do.

## Tests

Four new blocks in `tests/testthat/test-tree.R`, each confirmed to fail before the fix (5 failing assertions): a numeric and a character stump through `generate_case_when_tree()`, a v2 ranger parsed model with a stump tree through `tidypredict_fit()`, a parsed model whose `general` has no `mode`, and a class-label stump through `.build_case_when_tree()`.

`devtools::test()`: 0 failures, 2003 passing. `devtools::check()`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 note (the pre-existing `.git` hidden-directory note).

title: Read a randomForest stump without getTree
description:
Closes #362

A tree with a single root node and no split made `tidypredict_fit()` and `parse_model()` abort with "argument of length 0".

## Root cause

The error comes from `randomForest` itself, before any tidypredict code runs. `randomForest::getTree()` assembles the node table with `cbind()` and subsets it to the tree's node count without `drop = FALSE`. For a stump that count is 1, so the matrix collapses to a plain vector, `nrow()` returns `NULL`, and the `1:nrow(tree)` on the next line fails.

## Fix

Both call sites (`rf_tree_info_full()` for the `parse_model()` path and `build_nested_rf_tree()` for the direct `tidypredict_fit()` path) now go through `rf_get_tree()`, which delegates to `getTree()` for a tree with more than one node and assembles the same six columns itself for a stump. The parser and the nested formula builder already handled a terminal root node, so nothing downstream changed.

## Tests

Two tests in `tests/testthat/test-model-rf.R`, both comparing against `randomForest::predict()` on the direct and the parsed path, and both asserting the fit actually contains a stump. Verified they fail on the unpatched parser.

title: Name lda and nnet classes from the groups that were fit
description:
Closes #302

## Root cause

`MASS::lda()` and `nnet::nnet()` both drop an outcome level that no observation fell in (warning `group zzz is empty`), but they still keep the full level set in `model$lev`. `parse_model()` named the classes from `lev` while building one set of terms per fitted group, so the two lengths disagreed and `tidypredict_fit()` errored before returning anything.

## Before

```r
set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(120), x2 = runif(120))
d$g <- factor(sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 120, TRUE), levels = c("a", "b", "c", "zzz"))

tidypredict_fit(MASS::lda(g ~ x1 + x2, data = d))
#> Error in intercepts[[i]] : subscript out of bounds

tidypredict_fit(nnet::nnet(g ~ x1 + x2, data = d, size = 2, trace = FALSE))
#> Error: 'names' attribute [4] must be the same length as the vector [3]
```

## After

lda names its classes from `names(model$prior)`, and nnet, when it has more than one output unit, from `colnames(model$fitted.values)`. Those are what each package's own `predict()` labels its output with. A binary nnet has a single unnamed output unit and still uses `lev`.

Measured on `iris` with an extra unused `Species` level: both models now match their own `predict()` output exactly across all 150 rows (`predict(model, df)$posterior` for lda, `predict(model, df, type = "raw")` for nnet). The two new tests fail on `main` with the errors above and pass here; I verified that by reverting the two source files and re-running.

## Other consumers of `model$lev`

Checked and deliberately left alone:

- `nnet::multinom()` drops the empty level from `lev` itself, so it already agrees.
- `mda::fda()` already reads `rownames(model$means)`.
- `naivebayes::naive_bayes()` keeps the empty level in both its own `predict()` and the parsed model, so the two agree; there is nothing to fix.
- `MASS::qda()` refuses to fit at all: `some group is too small for 'qda'`.

## Checks

`devtools::test()`: 0 failures. `devtools::check()`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 note (the worktree's `.git` file).

One surprise worth flagging separately: `nnet:::predict.nnet(type = "class")` maps `max.col(z)` through the full `object$lev`, so when the empty level is not last (`levels = c("a", "zzz", "b", "c")`) nnet itself returns the wrong class labels. That is an upstream bug and is not touched here; tidypredict's probabilities are correctly labelled either way.

title: Handle one-column ksvm model matrices and scaling
description:
Closes #289.

kernlab drops names whenever a matrix or attribute vector has exactly one column, and `parse_model_ksvm()` indexed by name in two places.

**Terms dropped for a single-column model matrix.** `names(weights) <- colnames(xmatrix(model)[[1]])` was `NULL` for one column, so the loop over `names(linear)` ran zero times and the parsed model was nothing but an intercept. The names are now recovered from the non-response entries of the terms `dataClasses` when the matrix has one column (such a matrix can only come from one numeric predictor, since a factor expands to one dummy column per level), and a model whose predictor names cannot be recovered errors rather than silently losing every term.

**Scaling not undone when exactly one column was scaled.** `scaling(model)$x.scale[["scaled:center"]]` and `[["scaled:scale"]]` are unnamed in that case, because kernlab builds them from `attributes(x[, scaled])`. The `nm %in% names(scales)` test was then never true and the weights stayed on the scaled scale. Scaling is now undone positionally against `scaling(model)$scaled`, the logical vector aligned with the model-matrix columns. This shape is not exotic: kernlab does not scale dummy columns, so one numeric predictor plus any number of factors reaches it.

Maximum absolute difference from kernlab's own `predict()` on `mtcars`:

| model | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `eps-svr mpg ~ wt` | 10.97 | 3.6e-15 |
| `eps-svr mpg ~ wt + gear` | 14.59 | 7.1e-15 |
| `eps-svr mpg ~ wt + hp` | 7.1e-15 | 7.1e-15 |
| `eps-svr mpg ~ wt + hp + gear` | 3.6e-15 | 3.6e-15 |
| `C-svc am ~ wt` | 0.6105 | 3.3e-16 |
| `C-svc am ~ wt + gear` | 0.9419 | 2.2e-16 |
| `C-svc am ~ wt + hp` | 3.3e-16 | 3.3e-16 |
| `C-svc am ~ wt + hp + gear` | 6.7e-16 | 6.7e-16 |

The existing tests used two numeric predictors, which is why both bugs passed. The two new tests, one for regression and one for binary classification, cover the one-numeric and one-numeric-plus-factor shapes and were confirmed to fail (8 failures) with the fix reverted.

Also replaces `call. = FALSE` in `acceptable_formula.ksvm()` with `call = NULL`; `cli::cli_abort()` takes `call`, and the dotted name was swallowed by `...`.

title: Reject matrix-interface nnet fits
description:
Closes #303

`nnet::nnet(x, y)` (the `nnet.default()` matrix interface) produced a formula full of `NULL`:

```r
m <- nnet::nnet(as.matrix(mtcars[, c("wt","hp")]), mtcars$mpg, size = 2, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
tidypredict_fit(m)
#> 7.12 + case_when(-0.232 + NULL * 0.0177 + NULL * 5.878 < -15 ~ 0, ...
```

`parse_model.nnet()` took `vars <- names(attr(model$terms, "dataClasses")) %||% model$coefnames`, and for a default fit both are `NULL`. The dangerous part is that the expression does not error: it evaluates to a zero length numeric, so a wrong answer reads as an empty one.

## Abort rather than recover

The predictor names are not recoverable from the fitted object. `names(m)` is only `n`, `nunits`, `nconn`, `conn`, `nsunits`, `decay`, `entropy`, `softmax`, `censored`, `value`, `wts`, `convergence`, `fitted.values`, `residuals` and `call`: no `terms`, no `coefnames`, no `xlevels`. `dimnames(m$residuals)` names the rows and the output units, and its second element is `NULL` for a single output, so it never carries the input names. The names survive only inside the unevaluated `m$call`, which would mean re-evaluating user code in an unknown environment.

`predict.nnet()` itself matches inputs positionally for these fits, which tidypredict cannot do when it has to name columns of a data frame. So `parse_model()` now aborts with a message pointing at the formula interface.

## Other models on this code path

- `nnet::multinom()` has no matrix interface: `multinom(as.matrix(iris[, 1:4]), iris$Species)` errors inside `nnet` with "invalid formula", so `parse_model.multinom()` always has `terms`.
- parsnip: `fit_xy()` with the `nnet` engine builds a data frame before calling `nnet()`, so `model$fit$coefnames` is populated even when the user passes a matrix. Verified for both a data frame and a matrix `x`.

Both checked and clean.

## Tests

Added a snapshot test in `tests/testthat/test-model-nnet.R` next to the other rejection tests, covering both `tidypredict_fit()` and `parse_model()`. Confirmed it fails on the unfixed code (2 failures, "Expected ... to throw a error").

`devtools::test()`: 0 failures, 1997 passing. `devtools::check()`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 note (the `.git` file of the worktree).

title: Document the probit link's approximation
description:
Closes #355, taking option 1: document the approximation, leave the behaviour alone.

`apply_inverse_link()` writes the probit inverse link as the Bowling et al. logistic approximation to the normal CDF, because the exact form is `pnorm()` and no SQL backend has one. It is the only inexact inverse link in that `switch()`, and nothing anywhere said so.

Measured on `glm(am ~ wt + mpg, mtcars, family = binomial(link = "probit"))`:

- max abs diff vs `predict(type = "response")`: **1.39e-4**, matching the approximation's stated ~0.014% error
- `tidypredict_test()`: **31 of 32 rows** over the default threshold

So a user following the documented verification workflow sees a failure with no explanation available to them. That is what this fixes.

Adds a "The probit link" section to the glm article giving the formula, the measurement as a live chunk (so it cannot drift), and the `tidypredict_test()` output, plus a limitations bullet linking to it and a comment at the code explaining why the approximation is there.

`devtools::check()`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes.

title: Reject h2o models that are not GBM or RuleFit
description:
Closes #284.

Every h2o algorithm returns one of `H2ORegressionModel`, `H2OBinomialModel` or `H2OMultinomialModel`, so the class a model dispatches on says nothing about how it was fit, and nothing was reading `model@algorithm`. Only RuleFit was special-cased.

## Sweep

Ran every supervised algorithm the cluster registers through `tidypredict_fit()` and compared against `h2o.predict()` on `mtcars`, rather than only the ones named in the issue.

| algorithm | regression | binomial | multinomial |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gbm` | 4.3e-08 | 1.3e-09 | 1.5e-09 |
| `drf` | **130.8** | **0.982** | **0.243** |
| `glm` | error | error | |
| `deeplearning` | error | | |
| `naivebayes` | | error | |
| `gam` | error | | |
| `psvm` | | error | |
| `adaboost` | | error | |
| `isotonicregression` | error | | |
| `rulefit` | already handled | already handled | already rejected |

DRF is the one that matters: it returns a number rather than an error. h2o averages tree predictions where the code sums them, so regression is off by exactly the tree count, and classification uses vote proportions rather than a logistic link. Everything tree-free reports no trees, which surfaced as `seq_len(NULL)` complaining that its argument must be coercible to a non-negative integer.

## Fix

One `h2o_check_gbm()` helper, called from all three `tidypredict_fit()` methods after the RuleFit branch. Tests cover a DRF on each of the three classes plus a `glm` for the no-trees shape.

Two things found along the way but left alone, since neither is this issue:

- `h2o.decision_tree()` and `h2o.stackedEnsemble()` would not fit at all on this data, so they are untested. The guard covers them by construction.
- `tidypredict_test.H2OMultinomialModel()` indexes `preds[, domain]`, which fails when the outcome's levels look like numbers (h2o names those probability columns `p3`, `p4`, ...). Unrelated to the algorithm check, and only reachable with a GBM.

`devtools::check()`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes. Suite 1995 passing.

title: Support xgboost boosters that have been saved and reloaded
description:
Fixes #292.

## The defects

Two, in sequence, both hit by an ordinary `xgb.save()` / `xgb.load()` round trip:

1. **Wrong API path.** `attr(model, "param")` was the discriminator between the pre-2.0 and post-2.0 xgboost APIs, but `xgb.train()` sets that attribute and `xgb.load()` does not, so it records how the object was *made*, not which API is available. A reloaded booster took the legacy path and called `xgb.model.dt.tree(text = )`, an argument xgboost 3.x has removed: `argument "model" is missing, with no default`.

2. **Lost objective.** Past that, `params$objective` is `NULL` for a reloaded booster, so `apply_xgb_objective()` only warned and returned the raw margin. The user got logits presented as probabilities, behind a warning blaming a custom objective.

Gating on the installed xgboost version fixes the first; recovering the objective from the saved JSON, alongside the existing `base_score` extraction, fixes the second. Worth noting `params$objective` is `NULL` on xgboost 3.x for *trained* boosters too — the objective comes from `attr(model, "param")` there — so the JSON is the only source a reloaded booster has.

## Also fixed, as the issue asks

`get_xgb_trees_df()` never restored the row order after `merge(trees, feature_names_tbl, by = "Feature")`. `merge()` sorts by the join column, and the code below converts node IDs to row *positions* assuming row `i` holds node `i - 1`. Latent only because nothing reached that path; fixed alongside so that changing the discriminator cannot un-mask it.

## Verified

Five objectives, each trained and reloaded:

| | loaded vs trained | loaded vs `predict()` | parsed vs `predict()` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `reg:squarederror` | 0 | 1.36e-06 | 1.36e-06 |
| `binary:logistic` | 0 | 5.53e-08 | 5.53e-08 |
| `count:poisson` | 0 | 5.59e-07 | 5.59e-07 |
| `reg:tweedie` | 0 | 3.78e-06 | 3.78e-06 |
| `binary:logitraw` | 0 | 1.04e-07 | 1.04e-07 |

A reloaded booster is now bit-identical to the trained one through both the direct and the `parse_model()` path. The residual against `predict()` is xgboost's float32 accumulation floor, identical for trained and loaded.

## Tests

`test-model-xgboost.R` gains a round-trip test over three objectives, asserting the objective survives onto the parsed model and that the reloaded booster agrees with both the trained one and `predict()`. It errors without the fix.

title: Honour lightgbm sigmoid and reg_sqrt
description:
Closes the last two items of #288. Found by the ignored-fit-options battery from the open-bug triage plan.

## The defects

- **`sigmoid` was fixed at 1.** LightGBM's `binary` and `multiclassova` objectives apply `1 / (1 + exp(-sigmoid * x))`, so every probability of a model fit with any other value came out rescaled. Measured 0.141 off `predict()` at `sigmoid = 2`.
- **`reg_sqrt` was ignored.** It trains on `sqrt(|y|)` keeping the sign, and `ConvertOutput` squares the raw score back onto the response scale. Predictions were left on the square-root scale, measured 8.23 off.

## Two corrections to the issue

Both came from checking each objective against `predict()` rather than from the parameter list, and both would have been regressions if implemented as written:

- **`cross_entropy` accepts `sigmoid` but never applies it.** The issue lists it alongside `binary` as taking the scaling. It does not: its link is a plain logistic whatever the parameter says. Verified at sigmoid 1, 2 and 3 — `predict()` matches `logistic(raw)` exactly and `logistic(s * raw)` by 0.15 and 0.226. Scaling it would have broken a currently correct model.
- **`huber` accepts `reg_sqrt` but does not act on it.** The issue's fix applies the squaring to everything in `lgb_identity_objectives`. `huber` stays on the raw scale; squaring it is wrong by 90.7. The other five (`regression`, `regression_l2`, `regression_l1`, `fair`, `quantile`, `mape`) all honour it.

Both exceptions are now named constants with the reason recorded next to them.

## Verified

21 configurations, all exact (0 difference): `sigmoid` at 0.5, 1, 2, 3 across `binary`, `cross_entropy` and `multiclassova`; `reg_sqrt` across all six identity objectives; and a control for each.

## Tests

`test-model-lightgbm.R` gains three cases: a non-default `sigmoid` over several values, `reg_sqrt` over four objectives including `huber`, and a regression guard asserting `cross_entropy` stays unscaled. The first two fail without the fix.

Not addressed here, to keep this reviewable: the two cleanups #288 mentions in the same area (the dead `if` block and the unreachable `default_left` branch).

title: Reject glmnet models fit with an offset
description:
Fixes #296. Found by the ignored-fit-options battery from the open-bug triage plan.

## The defect

`parse_model_glmnet()` ignored `model$offset`, so the offset was silently dropped from the prediction. Measured 1.69 away from `predict(newoffset = ...)` on the battery's data, and the issue reports 7.47 on `mtcars`.

The offset cannot be reconstructed: glmnet stores only a logical flag on the fitted object, never the values, and `predict()` requires them again as `newoffset`. Aborting is the only correct action, as the issue concludes.

## Scope

The same hole was in the multinomial path (`parse_model_glmnet_multinom()`), which the issue does not mention. Both now go through one `glmnet_check_no_offset()` helper. Verified rejecting on gaussian, poisson and multinomial offsets.

Controls unaffected: poisson without an offset stays at 8.9e-16 and multinomial at 3.3e-16.

## Tests

`test-model-glmnet.R` gains snapshot tests for the single-outcome and multinomial cases, on both `tidypredict_fit()` and `parse_model()`.

title: Reject ranger probability and survival forests
description:
Fixes #301. Found by the ignored-fit-options battery from the open-bug triage plan.

## The defect

`parse_model.ranger()` and `tidypredict_fit_ranger_nested()` detected a classification forest by reading a leaf's prediction and testing whether it was a character. A probability or survival forest has no `prediction` column in `treeInfo()` at all, so that expression is `NULL`, `is.character(NULL)` is `FALSE`, and both slipped past.

The consequences differed by entry point, and neither was usable:

- `tidypredict_fit()` emitted `case_when(x <= 0.0066 ~ NULL, .default = NULL)` and failed later with an unrelated vctrs error.
- `parse_model()` returned a parsed model with no predictions and raised nothing at all.

Guarding on the forest type states the condition directly, with a message per unsupported type.

## One correction to the issue

The field is `treetype`, lowercase, not `treeType`. Worth flagging because the wrong spelling fails silently: `model$treeType` is `NULL`, so the guard never fires and, since it replaces the old leaf-value check, classification forests stop being rejected too. Caught by running the battery against the change rather than by reading it. The helper also falls back to `model$forest$treetype`.

Verified: probability, classification and survival all reject; regression and a parsnip regression fit are untouched at 0 difference.

## Tests

`test-model-ranger.R` gains snapshot tests for probability and survival forests, on both `tidypredict_fit()` and `parse_model()`. The v1/v2 parsed-model path now also treats a missing leaf value as unsupported rather than only a character one.

title: Honour an mboost mstop reduced after fitting
description:
Fixes #306. Found by the ignored-fit-options battery from the open-bug triage plan.

## The defect

`mboost_components()` pulls `ens` out of the predict closure and uses all of it. Subsetting a fitted model with `model[m]` — the standard `cvrisk()` then `model[mstop(cv)]` workflow — sets `mstop` in that same environment but leaves `ens` at its full length, so every boosting iteration was used regardless of what `mstop` reported.

Truncating `ens` to `mstop` fixes it. Raising `mstop` grows `ens`, so truncation is always the right operation.

## Measured

Max abs diff against `predict()`, on a 100-iteration `blackboost` subset to 30:

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model[30]` | 2.22 | 1.8e-15 |
| `model[50]` | (same cause) | 1.8e-15 |
| `model[100]`, i.e. no reduction | 3.6e-15 | 3.6e-15 |
| never subset | 3.6e-15 | 3.6e-15 |

## Tests

`test-model-mboost.R` gains a case that subsets a fitted model before parsing, asserting both the direct and the `parse_model()` path. Confirmed to fail without the fix.

The existing "blackboost respects mstop and nu" test sets `mstop` in `boost_control()` at fit time, which was always honoured; only a reduction *after* fitting hit this.

title: Resolve the split-boundary tie the way the model does
description:
Found by the threshold-precision battery from the open-bug triage plan: probe values at, just above and just below every split boundary in the generated formula, across every supported model class, and compare against each package's own `predict()`.

## The defect

`f32_split_boundary()` places the boundary at the exact midpoint between the stored 32-bit threshold and its adjacent float. That midpoint is itself representable as a double, so a value can sit precisely on it, and there the boundary cannot express what the model does: rounding the midpoint to a float is a tie, broken towards the even mantissa. When it resolves to the neighbour rather than to the threshold, the model reads the value as being on the far side of the split while the generated formula does not.

This is not a rare shape. About half of all thresholds resolve the tie towards the neighbour: over 20,000 random thresholds, 9,868 do, for both `side` values.

Nudging the boundary one double past the midpoint in those cases leaves every other value's branch untouched, because adjacent floats are roughly 2^29 doubles apart.

## Measured

Boundary probes on identical fitted models, before and after:

| Backend | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `xgboost` | 34 of 3348 probes differ, max 0.937 | 0 |
| `lightgbm` | 0 of 684 | 0 |
| `catboost` | 0 of 1212 | 0 |

One `model-cubist` snapshot moves by one double ULP (`95.1000022888184` to `95.1000022888183`).

## On the two backends still failing the battery

`Cubist::cubist()` and `C50::C5.0()` still show probe failures, and they are artifacts of the battery rather than defects. Both packages' `predict()` serialise `newdata` to a text file via `makeDataFile()`, which formats with `format(x, digits = 15)`, so neither ever sees the full double. Every failing probe row was confirmed to have its value moved by that round trip, and with probes no finer than 15 significant digits Cubist passes 0 of 96 at its own float noise floor (3e-07). Worth recording that the format is chosen per column, so the precision either package sees for one value depends on the other rows in the same batch.

## Tests

- `test-float32.R` gains two property tests: a value on the boundary takes the branch the model's float comparison takes, and the boundary separates the floats either side of it. Over 200 random thresholds for both `side` values.
- `test-model-xgboost.R` gains a probe over every threshold in the generated formula, at the boundary and one double either side.

Both were checked against a build with only the tie adjustment disabled, and both fail there. The xgboost test deliberately does not use `mtcars`: none of the thresholds xgboost picks there resolve the tie towards the neighbour, so the probe passes with or without the fix. That is the same trap recorded earlier for C5.0, where a single small model found nothing.

title: Vote boosted C5.0 trials with the right confidence
description:
Closes #287.

The float32 cut item was fixed in #326. Of the remaining three, two hold up and one does not.

### Boosted confidence

`PredictBoostClassify()` adds `Confidence` to the vote of the class each trial predicts, and `PredictTreeClassify()` reports that as `(freq + prior) / (n_leaf + 1)`, where `prior` is the class proportion at the root of **that trial's own tree**. The parser used the Laplace ratio `(freq + 1) / (n_leaf + 2)`.

Sweeping 720 configurations (3 class counts × ordered and unordered × 2 sample sizes × 10 seeds × trials {1,2,3,5,10} × rules {T,F}) against `predict(type = "class")`:

| | wrong |
|---|---|
| before | **72 / 720** |
| after | **4 / 720** |

Every one of the 72 was a boosted model. `trials = 1` and the rules path were already exact, which is why the existing tests are green.

A tie in the total vote now goes to the default class rather than the first level, matching `SelectClass` and what the rules path already did.

### The leaf argmax item does not hold up

The issue reports that a leaf's class should be the argmax of its frequencies rather than the class it records. I implemented that and the sweep got **worse**, so I tested five readings of it against `predict()` across 80 boosted configurations:

| leaf class rule | wrong |
|---|---|
| the class the leaf records (kept) | **1 / 80** |
| argmax of `(freq + prior_trial)`, incumbent = default class | 15 / 80 |
| argmax of `(freq + prior_trial)`, incumbent = first level | 15 / 80 |
| argmax of `(freq + prior_trial)`, incumbent = stored class | 15 / 80 |
| argmax of `(freq + prior_first_tree)`, incumbent = default class | 18 / 80 |

So `predict(type = "class")` returns the recorded leaf class in both the single-tree and the boosted path. The seed 24 example in the issue is real but misdiagnosed: the leaf that trips it has *tied* frequencies (`3.14943,3.14943`), and none of the five rules above reproduces what decides such a leaf. Those tied leaves are the residual 4 of 720, and I have left them rather than guess.

Worth recording that C5.0's two prediction types genuinely disagree here. On a leaf with `class="c2" freq="0,1,1"` and priors `0.335,0.33,0.335`, the class probabilities are `0.11167 / 0.44333 / 0.445`, so `type = "prob"` puts `c3` highest while `type = "class"` returns `c2`. tidypredict reproduces both, separately.

### The `[ordered]` marker

`c50_attr_levels()` did return `"[ordered]lo"` as the first level of an ordered predictor, and that is fixed. It is unreachable today, though: the list is only consulted for a `type="1"` multiway split, and across 160 fits spanning 3 to 6 levels, `subset` both ways and several signal strengths, C5.0 never emitted `type="1"` for an ordered predictor. It splits them as `type="3"`, which reads its levels from `elts` instead. The fix therefore has a unit test on the helper rather than an end-to-end one, and I have asked on the issue for the model behind the reported 88/400.

### Smaller items

A level containing `,` makes `C5.0()` exit and write no tree at all, so the reported `subscript out of bounds` came from indexing an empty tree rather than from the level lookup. Both are now guarded, and the model-with-no-tree case is reported clearly.

`R CMD check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes. The one suite failure is h2o's cluster failing to start, which has been intermittent all session and is unrelated.

title: Write the softmax so it cannot overflow
description:
Closes #299.

`expr_softmax()` emitted `exp(s_k) / sum(exp(s_j))`, which is `Inf / Inf` and so `NaN` once any class score passes about 710. Every reference implementation subtracts the row maximum first, so they returned a valid distribution where tidypredict returned nothing usable.

### Not `pmax()`

The issue suggested building the row maximum and subtracting it. That works, but `pmax(s_1, ..., s_K)` inlines every score expression once more inside each of the `K` results, taking the formula from `O(K²)` to `O(K³)` in the number of classes: about 12 times larger for a ten-class model.

Subtracting `s_k` instead gives the algebraically identical

```
p_k = 1 / sum_j exp(s_j - s_k)
```

which is just as overflow-safe, only about twice the size, and needs no `pmax()` or `GREATEST()`, so there is no SQL question to answer. The `j == k` term is `exp(0)`, written as the literal `1`, so the denominator is never below 1 and cannot underflow to zero either. A score far above the rest sends the other terms to `Inf`, giving `1 / Inf = 0`, which is the right limit.

### Sweep

Ten affected classes, six rows ranging from an ordinary iris row to `±1000` in every predictor. Count of rows where any class probability is `NaN`:

| class | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `MASS::lda` | 4 | **0** |
| `MASS::qda` | 4 | **0** |
| `mda::fda` | 4 | **0** |
| `sparsediscrim::lda_diag` | 4 | **0** |
| `sparsediscrim::lda_shrink_mean` | 4 | **0** |
| `klaR::NaiveBayes` | 4 | **0** |
| `naivebayes::naive_bayes` | 4 | **0** |
| `nnet::multinom` | 3 | **0** |
| multinomial `glmnet` | 1 | **0** |
| `nnet::nnet` | 0 | 0 |

`h2o`, `lightgbm` and `catboost` share the same helper.

### One divergence, deliberately

`mda::fda` and the `sparsediscrim` family normalize with the textbook form themselves, so **their own `predict()` returns `NaN` on those rows**. tidypredict used to match them by also returning `NaN`; it now returns the distribution the class scores imply.

This is the same shape as the naive Bayes `threshold` case documented for #300: reproducing a floating point artifact of the reference is not worth doing, and the answer tidypredict gives is the one every other backend gives for the same scores. It has a test in `test-model-sparsediscrim.R` that asserts both halves, the reference's `NaN` and tidypredict's finite distribution, plus a check that ordinary rows still match exactly.

For `klaR` and `naivebayes` the extreme rows now fall under the already-documented `threshold` divergence, which they previously could not reach because the result was `NaN` before the comparison mattered.

### Tests

- `expr_softmax survives scores that would overflow (#299)` in `test-misc.R`, including that adding a constant to every score leaves the result unchanged, which is the property the old form lost.
- `a row far outside the training range matches predict() (#299)` in `test-model-lda.R`.
- The divergence test above.

Two naive Bayes snapshots updated for the new formula text. `R CMD check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes.

title: Route LightGBM missing values by missing_type
description:
Closes the two missing-value items of #288.

Both turned out to be the same mechanism. `Tree::NumericalDecision` consults `default_left` only when the node's `missing_type` is `NaN` or `Zero`:

| `missing_type` | when you get it | what LightGBM does |
|---|---|---|
| `NaN` | feature had a missing value in training | `default_left` decides |
| `None` | feature had none, the common case | missing value coerced to `0.0`, compared normally |
| `Zero` | `zero_as_missing = TRUE` | an exact zero is missing too, `default_left` decides |

The parser routed purely by `default_left`, so it was right only for `NaN`, which is exactly what every existing test happened to produce: they all train *with* NA and `use_missing = TRUE`.

`lgb.model.dt.tree()` does not report `missing_type`, so `add_lgb_missing_type()` reads it from the JSON dump and joins it on by tree and split index.

For `None` the emitted condition does not need `coalesce()`: the threshold is known at build time, so `is.na(col) | col <= val` or `!is.na(col) & col <= val` is chosen depending on which side `0` falls, which also keeps the formula translatable.

### Sweep

12 configurations by 3 seeds, max absolute difference against `predict()`, on data with missing values, exact zeros and a categorical feature. Both the direct and parsed paths, which agreed on every row.

| config | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| regression, train NA | 0 | 0 |
| regression, no NA | 5.64 | **0** |
| regression, `use_missing = FALSE` | 11.6 | **0** |
| regression, `zero_as_missing` | 5.09 | **0** |
| regression, `zero_as_missing` + train NA | 1.13 | **0** |
| binary | 0.541 | **0** |
| binary, `zero_as_missing` | 0.537 | **0** |
| multiclass | 0.595 | **2.2e-16** |
| multiclass, `zero_as_missing` | 0.571 | **2.2e-16** |
| poisson | 3.22 | **0** |
| `boosting = "rf"` | 9.47 | **0** |
| `linear_tree` | 5.74 | **5.3e-15** |

### A third fault

A categorical split carried a missing value left when `default_left` was set. `Tree::CategoricalDecision` sends a missing value right whatever `default_left` says, so that branch was wrong wherever it fired. Two existing tests asserted the wrong shape by matching `is.na` against the deparsed formula; both are now behavioural checks of which branch a missing value actually takes.

### Found while sweeping

**#346**, unrelated to missing values: a `linear_tree` model fits fine directly but errors once it has been through `parse_model()`, because `build_nested_from_flat_paths()` reads `$prediction`, which is `NULL` for every linear leaf. A saved linear-tree model therefore cannot be loaded and used. Present before this work, confirmed on `main`.

`R CMD check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes.

title: Reject unsupported contrasts for lda, qda and fda models
description:
Closes #343.

`MASS::lda()`, `MASS::qda()` and `mda::fda()` all call `acceptable_formula()`, which routes to `acceptable_lm()`, whose contrast check reads `model$contrasts`. None of the three records that field, so the check was a no-op.

An ordered factor expands into columns named `f.L`, `f.Q` and `f.C`. `parse_label_lm()` recovers `".L"` as the level and emits a comparison no row matches, so the term was silently dropped. There was no error, just wrong posterior probabilities:

| class | unordered factor | ordered, before | ordered, after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MASS::lda` | 2.2e-16 | **0.625** | aborts |
| `MASS::qda` | 1.2e-15 | **0.848** | aborts |
| `mda::fda` | 3.3e-16 | **0.630** | aborts |

Max absolute difference against each package's own `predict()`.

### Two checks, because the models differ in what they record

`lda` and `qda` store `xlevels`, and expose the expanded names as `colnames(model$means)`, so they use the `acceptable_contrasts()` that #323 added for `earth`. That is exact for any contrast: it rejects `contr.sum` on an unordered factor as readily as `contr.poly` on an ordered one, and both cases have a test.

`fda` stores neither the contrasts nor the levels, anywhere on the object. With nothing to compare the expanded names against, the check falls back to `acceptable_ordered()`, which rejects a predictor whose `dataClasses` entry is `"ordered"`. That covers the case that reaches the parser in practice, since R gives an ordered factor `contr.poly` unless the global option says otherwise. It has two known edges, both preferable to the silent wrong answer:

- a global `options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", ...))` on an *unordered* factor is still missed for `fda` (0.585 off), where `lda` and `qda` now catch it;
- an ordered factor under a global *treatment* contrast is rejected although it would have worked.

The response is excluded from that check, so an ordered *outcome* is not mistaken for an ordered predictor. That has a test as well.

### One fix to the shared helper

`acceptable_contrasts()` now splits an interaction column on `:` before matching, the way `parse_label_lm()` does. Without it `mpg:wt` was read as variable `mpg` with level `":wt"` and rejected, which broke the existing "interactions are handled" tests for `lda` and `qda`. Caught by the suite, not by the sweep.

### Swept alongside

`kernlab::ksvm` (8.9e-16) and the four `sparsediscrim` classes are unaffected by an ordered factor. `xrf::xrf()` refuses to fit one upstream, in its own `correct_xgb_sparse_categoricals()`.

`R CMD check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes.

title: Reject unsupported contrasts for earth models
description:
Closes #323.

`parse_model.earth()` never called `acceptable_formula()`, so an ordered factor, which R fits with `contr.poly` by default, was parsed as if the polynomial contrast values were the column itself. The formula that came out compared the factor against values such as `-0.2236` and failed with "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed".

Adding the call is not enough on its own: `earth` records no `contrasts` field, so `acceptable_lm()`'s check has nothing to read and stays a no-op.

### How the contrast is recovered instead

The new `acceptable_contrasts(columns, vars, xlevels)` in `R/acceptable.R` reads the contrast back off the names the model gave the columns each factor expanded into. Only the treatment contrast names those after the levels themselves, which is exactly what the parser assumes when it recovers a level from a column name:

| contrast | columns for a four-level `f` | accepted |
|---|---|---|
| `contr.treatment` | `fb`, `fc`, `fd` | yes |
| `contr.poly` (ordered, the default) | `f.L`, `f.Q`, `f.C` | no |
| `contr.sum` | `f1`, `f2`, `f3` | no |

A column is assigned to the longest matching variable, the same rule `parse_label_lm()` uses, so #290's nested prefix names (`x`, `xy`, `xyz`) are not misread as levels of one another.

An `x`/`y` fit records neither a formula nor `xlevels`, so there is nothing to check and it is left alone. That path is already covered by the existing tests.

### Sweep

An ordered factor across the linear family, max absolute difference against each package's own `predict()`:

| class | unordered | ordered, before | ordered, after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lm`, `glm`, `rq`, `nnet`, `multinom` | ~1e-15 | aborts | aborts |
| `earth` | 4.4e-16 | **nonsense formula** | aborts |

`contr.sum` on an *unordered* factor was a second, quieter case: the level recovered from `f1` matches no row, so the term silently drops out rather than erroring. It is now rejected too, and has its own test.

### Found while sweeping

`MASS::lda`, `MASS::qda` and `mda::fda` have the same hole, and there it is silent rather than an error: they record no `contrasts` either, and produce posteriors off by 0.63, 0.85 and 0.63 on an ordered factor with no complaint. Filed as **#343**, to be fixed with the same helper. `kernlab::ksvm` and the four `sparsediscrim` classes were swept at the same time and are unaffected; `xrf::xrf()` refuses to fit an ordered factor upstream.

`R CMD check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes.

title: Take CatBoost category hashes from CatBoost's own hash function
description:
Closes #297.

`set_catboost_categories()` needs to know which category each hash in a saved model stands for. It discovered that by training one probe model per category and reading back the split the probe chose, recording a mapping only when the probe's `features_info` happened to hold exactly one hash. That works for a three-level factor, which is the only level count the tests covered.

CatBoost does not hide its hash function from R. `catboost.load_pool()` hashes a factor column itself, with the registered routine `CatBoostHashStrings_R`, and hands the result to the pool as a double whose bits are the 32-bit hash reinterpreted as a 32-bit float. Reading those bits back as an integer gives exactly the value the saved model records, so the mapping is exact, needs no probe models, and does not depend on what a probe happens to split on.

The probe machinery is gone: five functions and about 90 lines replaced by two.

### What the sweep found

7 level counts (2 to 8) by 8 seeds, comparing `tidypredict_fit()` against `catboost.predict()`:

| levels | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 3 wrong (max diff 2.25), 5 errors | 8 exact |
| 3 | 8 exact | 8 exact |
| 4 to 8 | 40 errors | 40 exact |

Max difference across all 56 configurations is now 0, not merely within tolerance. The parsnip/bonsai path, which routes through the same function, was swept separately at 2, 4, 5, 6 and 8 levels and is also exact.

The two-level column is the part the issue did not describe. Those three configurations did not error: they produced a mapping with the two levels **the wrong way round** and predicted silently wrong. The old `fill_catboost_hash_mapping()` assigned the one leftover category to the one leftover hash whenever exactly one of each remained, which for a two-level factor is reachable with nothing checked.

### Failing loudly

As the issue asks, a hash that cannot be named now aborts in `set_catboost_categories()`:

```
Error in `build_catboost_hash_mapping()`:
! Cannot name 4 categories of "cat_feat".
i `data` must have the levels the model was fit on.
```

Previously an unmapped hash was recorded as `NA` and surfaced much later, from `build_nested_catboost_categorical()` at fit time.

### Tests

- `categorical predictions match for any level count (#297)`, looping 2 through 8 against `catboost.predict()`.
- `set_catboost_categories errors on levels the model never saw (#297)`, a snapshot of the new abort.

`R CMD check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes.

title: Document the naive Bayes zero-density divergence
description:
Closes the `threshold` item of #300.

`klaR::NaiveBayes()` and `naivebayes::naive_bayes()` both evaluate each normal density and then replace any that came out as exactly zero with their `threshold` argument, `0.001` by default. tidypredict works on the log scale, where nothing underflows, so the substitution never happens. The decision was whether to reproduce it or document it. Documented.

### Why documenting is the better answer, not just the cheaper one

The substitution does not degrade gracefully. It flips the prediction to the *worst*-fitting class. On the iris model with a `Sepal.Length` of 20:

|                | setosa    | versicolor | virginica  |
| -------------- | --------- | ---------- | ---------- |
| `predict()`    | **1**     | 7.5e-176   | 9.1e-118   |
| `tidypredict`  | 0         | 8.3e-59    | **1**      |

`setosa` has the narrowest spread of the three, so at roughly 42 standard deviations out its density is the first to underflow. Replacing it with `0.001` makes it enormous next to the other two, which were computed honestly. Both packages behave identically here.

This is silent. The only case either package warns about is when *every* class underflows, by which point all three posteriors are meaningless anyway.

### Why it could not be reproduced faithfully

The substitution keys off a floating point underflow, not off anything in the model. Testing `exp(log_density) == 0` instead of `density == 0` selects a different set of values: over 200,000 draws from the band where the underflow happens, the two tests disagree on about 1,000 of them, because the two routes round differently in the denormal range. A SQL backend, working in its own floating point, would disagree again in a third way. Reproducing it would trade a divergence that can be stated in a paragraph for one that cannot.

### Changes

- A section in the naive Bayes article, with the comparison above as live chunks so it cannot silently rot.
- A comment at each of the two `threshold` definitions, distinguishing the categorical use (reproduced) from the density use (not).
- A test pinning the divergence, and asserting that data the model could actually have seen still matches `predict()` exactly.
- A NEWS bullet.

`R CMD check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes.

title: Apply the per-rule extrapolation limits for Cubist models
description:
Closes #285.

Cubist holds each rule's linear model to the span of the training outcomes that rule covers, recorded in the model text as the rule's `loval` and `hival`, widened at both ends by the model's `extrap` times that span. tidypredict never read those fields, so a rule's linear model was free to run away.

### The rule

Reverse-engineered by probing `predict()` on a grid and matching the saturation points against the model text, then confirmed with a reference implementation:

- Each rule's value is clamped to `[Lo - extrap * (Hi - Lo), Hi + extrap * (Hi - Lo)]`.
- The widened end never crosses zero. When `Lo >= 0` the lower bound is `max(0, ...)`, and symmetrically when `Hi <= 0`. A rule that only ever saw non-negative outcomes cannot be extrapolated into negative ones.
- Clamping is per rule and happens *before* rules are averaged. A row on which two rules fire gets the mean of two clamped values, not a clamp of the mean.

The zero rule is the part that is not guessable from the field names, and the ordering is confirmed rather than assumed: in one case the observed upper saturation of 29.201 is exactly the mean of two rules' individual upper bounds of 28.833 and 29.568.

### Not only about extrapolation

The issue title says extrapolation, but the clamp engages on ordinary rows of the training data. This turned up while fixing #322: seven of that PR's 90 sweep configurations still disagreed by up to 0.22 on the data the model was fitted to, including a row where `predict()` returns exactly `0` and the unclamped formula gives `-0.16`.

### Verification

- The #322 factor sweep, 15 seeds x {2, 3, 6} levels x {1, 5} committees, unordered and ordered, both code paths: from up to 0.22 down to 1.2e-6.
- A numeric sweep, 20 seeds x {1, 3, 10} committees, evaluated both on the training data and on newdata spanning +/-40 where the clamp does all the work: 2.0e-6.

Both residuals are the float32 arithmetic every Cubist model already carries.

### Notes

`pmin`/`pmax` render as `LEAST`/`GREATEST` under dbplyr. dbplyr warns that SQL always drops nulls there, so `na.rm = TRUE` is stated explicitly: it is what the SQL does either way, and it keeps the two backends agreeing. A rule with a constant prediction is clamped at parse time, so such a rule stays a plain number in the formula rather than gaining a `pmin(pmax(...))` around a literal.
