title: Support factor predictors in Cubist models
description:
Closes #322.

`parse_model.cubist()` read each rule's conditions from `model$splits`. That data frame is an incomplete record of what the model actually says, in two ways:

- It keeps the categorical column name quoted, so `f` arrives as `"f"` and is backtick-quoted into a name that does not exist.
- It only holds numeric (`type="2"`) and subset (`type="3"`) conditions. A rule that names a *single* level is written as `type="1"` and is missing from `model$splits` entirely.

The first is what the issue reports: the formula cannot be evaluated at all. The second is quieter and worse. With a rule's only condition dropped, the rule has no conditions left, is treated as unconditional, and applies to every row. A two-level factor produces wrong numbers rather than an error, which is how this got past the suite.

The fix reads conditions from the model text, the same source `Cubist`'s own `predict()` reads, so all three condition types are decoded from one place. `type="1"` and `type="3"` both become the existing `"set"` path type, which already emits `%in%`. A subset condition writes one quoted level per member, so parsing quoted tokens rather than splitting on commas keeps a level containing a comma in one piece.

### Verification

Swept 15 seeds x {2, 3, 6} levels x {1, 5} committees, with both an unordered and an ordered factor, on the direct and parsed paths. Before: an error, or silently wrong by up to 12.7. After: max abs difference from `predict()` of ~6e-7, which is the float32 residual every Cubist model already carries.

Seven of those 90 configurations still disagree by up to 0.22, and that turned out to be #285, the per-rule extrapolation clamp, not this. A reference implementation with the clamp added reproduces `predict()` to 1e-6 on all 90, so #285 is next and the residual here is understood rather than unexplained. The multi-committee test uses a seed where the clamp does not engage.

`R CMD check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes.

title: Support partykit splits with more than two branches
description:
Closes #295, the last of its three items.

Only `kids[[1]]` and `kids[[2]]` were kept, so every branch after the second was dropped: silently for a factor split, and with a "number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length" warning for a numeric one.

Took the generalisation the issue suggested rather than the abort, since an n-way `case_when` is the natural representation.

A node now carries an optional `branches` entry holding the kids in interval order and one condition per kid, and `build_multiway_node()` emits a clause for each. Two things fall out of `case_when` semantics that keep this small:

- Clauses are tried in order, so each condition only has to separate its kid from the kids *after* it. An interval split needs an upper bound, not both bounds.
- The last kid needs no condition at all; it is the `.default`.

Binary nodes do not go near this path, so rpart, ranger and randomForest are untouched. `branches` is only populated for nodes with three or more kids.

Covers all the multiway forms: a factor split with one kid per level (`index` names the kid), a numeric split with several breaks, and an ordered factor with several breaks. `right` is honoured throughout, so it composes with the fix in #337.

Verified at **max abs diff 0** for a hand-built 3-way numeric split in both `right` settings, and across 12 seeds x 3 formulas of `ctree(multiway = TRUE)` mixing unordered factors, ordered factors and numerics, on both the direct and parsed paths. The earlier binary sweep from #337 still reports 0. A multiway model also survives the YAML round trip.

title: Fix partykit split decoding
description:
Two of the three items in #295, plus a fourth fault the issue does not mention. The multiway item is left for a follow-up, since it needs a change to the shared tree generator rather than to the parser.

**`right` was ignored** (#295 item 1). `partysplit` records which end of the interval the break belongs to; with `right = FALSE` the left branch is `x < break`. Carried into the split info as `strict`, reusing the mechanism already there for rpart.

**Ordered factors errored** (#295 item 3). `class()` of an ordered factor is `c("ordered", "factor")`, so `map_chr(model$data, class)` failed on the length, and the `== "factor"` test would have miscounted it as continuous even without that. Now tested with `is.factor()`/`is.ordered()`. `partykit` splits an ordered factor with a break on the level's integer code, so it is recorded as the set of levels the break reaches, and `right` decides whether the level on the break itself is included.

**`index` was ignored for splits with a break.** Not in the issue, and the more serious of the three. With a break, `partysplit$index` maps each interval to a kid, and it is not always the identity: `partykit::as.party.rpart()` writes `2, 1`, putting the interval below the break on the *second* kid. Taking the kids in order swaps **both branches of every converted rpart tree**. `as.party(rpart(mpg ~ wt + disp + hp, mtcars))` was wrong on all 32 rows, max abs diff 13.93.

I found this only because the `right = FALSE` fix sent me to check a real object that produces such splits, rather than the hand-built `partysplit` in the issue. On main it reproduces identically, so it is pre-existing and not a regression from the other two fixes.

Verified at **max abs diff 0** across 15 seeds x 4 formulas x both code paths, for `ctree()` and for `as.party(rpart())`, with numeric, ordered-factor and unordered-factor predictors. `cforest` and `blackboost` agree to floating-point noise (7.1e-15), and `.extract_partykit_classprob()` to 0.

title: Decode ranger factor splits
description:
Closes #283.

`ranger` writes a split on a factor predictor in one of two forms, neither of which is a threshold on the column itself:

- **Ordered predictor** (`forest$is.ordered[j]`, covering `respect.unordered.factors = "ignore"` and `"order"` as well as genuinely ordered factors): the split value names a position in `forest$covariate.levels[[j]]`, and everything up to that position goes left. Under `"order"` those levels are *not* in the factor's own order, since `ranger` sorts them by mean response, so the stored order is the one to use.
- **Unordered predictor** (`"partition"`): the split value is a comma-separated list of level indices going **right**. Left is the complement.

Both the direct `tidypredict_fit()` path and the parsed-model path are fixed.

**Missing values needed a rule I did not expect.** After fixing the decoding, complete data matched exactly but rows with a missing factor still disagreed under `"partition"` only. Sending them left (the existing rule from #294, correct for numeric and ordered splits) gave max diff 2.92; sending them right gave 0.034, close enough to look like a rounding problem but not zero.

Tracing a disagreeing node showed why. An unordered split indexes a bitmask by the level's position, and a missing value collapses to the position of the **first level**, so the row goes wherever the first level goes at that node. That is not a fixed side: it looked like "always right" across 60 root splits only because the first level happened to be on the right in all of them. At a node splitting `3` out of four levels, it goes left.

Verified at **max abs diff 0** across 25 seeds x 3 modes x both code paths, with 2 to 8 level factors, an ordered factor, a numeric predictor, missing values in each, and rows missing every predictor. Also 0 for a probability forest via `.extract_ranger_classprob()`.

title: Decode randomForest factor splits
description:
Closes #282.

`randomForest` encodes a split on a factor predictor in one of two ways, and neither is a threshold on the column itself:

- **Unordered factor** (`forest$ncat > 1`): the split point is an integer whose bits name the levels going left. A split point of 10 on levels `a, b, c, d` means `{b, d}` go left. Comparing `f <= 10` against the factor warns and returns garbage.
- **Ordered factor** (`ncat == 1`): an ordinary numeric split point, but compared against the level's integer code. `o <= 2.5` against an ordered factor returns `NA` for every row, silently.

The unordered case is expressed as the set of levels going left, which the shared categorical split machinery already handled. The ordered case stays a numeric comparison, against `as.integer(col)`, because `randomForest` writes a `0` into `forest$xlevels` for anything that is not an unordered factor and so stores no levels to build a set from. An ordered factor is therefore only identifiable from the model's terms; a fit made through the `x`/`y` interface carries no terms, and in that case it is left alone.

Both the direct `tidypredict_fit()` path and the parsed-model path are fixed, so they agree.

Verified against `randomForest::predict()` at **max abs diff 0** for: an unordered factor, an ordered factor, both together, numeric-only (unchanged), a 20-level factor, the `x`/`y` interface, and `.extract_rf_classprob()` class probabilities.

title: Skip missing naive Bayes features instead of returning NA
description:
Closes two of the three items in #300.

**Missing values and unseen factor levels.** Both references skip a feature whose value is missing rather than failing the whole row: klaR returns `rep(1, length(apriori))` for it, naivebayes sets the density to `1`. A log density of `0` is a density of `1`, so the fix is `.default = 0` for the categorical `case_when()`, an explicit `is.na()` arm for the logical one, and an `ifelse(is.na(col), 0, ...)` wrapper on the numeric and Poisson terms. `klaR::predict.NaiveBayes()` coerces an unseen factor level to `NA`, which takes the same skip path, so that case is covered by the same change. A row missing every predictor now falls back on the class prior alone, matching both references.

The wrapper tests the column rather than the term, so that an `NA` arising from a degenerate fitted parameter still propagates rather than being silently swallowed. That matters for the second item.

The code comment claiming the old behaviour "matches the `NA` that `predict.NaiveBayes()` returns for them" was factually wrong and is replaced.

**A class with fewer than two observations.** `if (sd <= 0)` on an `NA` standard deviation raised "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" at parse time. Guarded with `!is.na(sd) &&`, so the `NA` is carried through and the fitted expression returns the `NA` probabilities that `predict()` returns for every row of such a fit.

Verified against both references on missing numeric, factor, logical and Poisson predictors, on all-missing rows, on unseen factor levels, and on the degenerate fit. All agree to `2.2e-16`.

**Not addressed here: the `threshold` item.** It reproduces, and worse than filed: on a sweep of 400 outlier rows against `klaR::NaiveBayes(Species ~ ., iris)` the worst row is a full class flip, not a small numeric difference. But it is not faithfully reproducible. klaR clamps with `prob[prob == 0] <- threshold`, which fires exactly when `dnorm()` underflows to zero in double precision. That boundary is not the same as `exp(log density) == 0`: over 200,000 probes across the denormal range the two disagree on 98. Emulating C-level double underflow inside generated SQL would diverge again per backend. This needs a decision between replicating it approximately and documenting the divergence, so I have left it open on the issue.

title: Substitute training means for missing predictors in Cubist
description:
Part of #294.

`Cubist` handles a missing value by substituting the predictor's training mean, which it writes into its own model text as `att="x" mean="..."`. It applies the substitution everywhere the predictor appears, in the rule conditions as well as in the linear models, so `tidypredict` has to do the same to match `predict()`.

`cubist_attribute_means()` reads those means straight out of the model text rather than recomputing them from the training data, because the rounded value is the one the C code reads back and predicts from. `substitute_missing_means()` then walks the fitted expression and replaces each predictor symbol with `ifelse(is.na(x), mean, x)`.

Verified across 11,376 rows and 30 models with 1 to 3 committees, checking two claims separately: that `Cubist::predict()` on a row with `NA` equals `predict()` on the same row with the mean filled in, and that `tidypredict` does the same. Both differences are exactly 0, so the substitution is correct by construction.

While verifying this I found a separate, pre-existing `Cubist` defect unrelated to missing values, where `predict()` returns exactly `0` for a complete row that satisfies a rule. It is filed separately and is not addressed here.

title: Send missing predictors down the left branch for ranger
description:
Part of #294, covering `ranger::ranger()`. Like `rpart` and unlike the partykit family, `ranger` resolves a missing value deterministically, so this reproduces what it does rather than returning `NA`.

The rule is a side effect of how it compares: `ranger` tests `value > splitval` to send a row right, and a missing value fails that test, so it takes the same branch as a value at or below the split point. Confirmed against `predict()` rather than read off the source, and it holds for every configuration I tried (regression, classification, probability forests, and both `respect.unordered.factors` settings).

This also swaps the `na_propagate` boolean added in #330 for a three-way `missing` argument. A second boolean would not have expressed which of the three behaviours a caller wanted, and there are now three: take the `.default` branch, return `NA`, or go left.

## Test plan

A randomised sweep over 40 forests varying tree count and `min.node.size`, with missing values scattered across every predictor plus rows missing all of them: **0 mismatches against `predict()` across 11,431 rows**. Both the fitted and the parsed/saved paths are covered, since ranger builds them through different code.

Note for anyone running a similar sweep: ranger models with a **factor** predictor disagree with `predict()` on complete data too, around 170 of 276 rows in one case. That is the pre-existing factor-decoding bug (#295, group A) and is untouched here, so factor models have to be excluded to see the missing-value behaviour cleanly.

```r
Rscript -e "devtools::test(filter = '^model-ranger$')"
```

title: Route missing values through rpart surrogate splits
description:
Part of #294, covering `rpart::rpart()` and, for free, `baguette::bagger()` with the `"CART"` base model. Unlike the rest of group C, `rpart` resolves a missing value deterministically, so this reproduces what it does rather than returning `NA`.

Most of the groundwork was already there: `rpart_tree_info_full()` has been extracting surrogates, the majority direction and `usesurrogate` all along. Nothing consumed them, so every missing value took the `.default` branch. This wires them into the expression and adds the one piece that was missing, what happens when no surrogate resolves the row.

Two things worth a look while reviewing:

The direction is built as a single `TRUE`/`FALSE` expression that the two subtrees hang off, rather than nesting a copy of the subtrees under each surrogate. The nested form is the obvious way to write it and grows the expression as `(surrogates + 1) ^ depth`, which is unusable at the default `maxsurrogate = 5`. A 25-node tree with 14 surrogates comes out at ~2 KB.

A tie between the two children is not a majority. `rpart` stops at the node and returns its own fitted value even under `usesurrogate = 2`, which I only found because a 250/250 split disagreed; ties are common in small or synthetic data.

## Test plan

Beyond the added tests, I ran a randomised sweep over 60 trees with `usesurrogate`, `cp`, `minsplit` and `maxsurrogate` all varied, missing values scattered across every predictor plus rows missing all of them: **0 mismatches against `predict()` across 15,691 rows**, with 22 tied internal nodes exercised. Categorical predictors and classification trees are exact too.

```r
Rscript -e "devtools::test(filter = '^model-(rpart|bagger)$')"
```

title: Return NA for missing predictors in the partykit family
description:
Part of #294, covering `partykit::ctree()`, `partykit::cforest()` and `mboost::blackboost()`.

These three cannot be fixed the way the issue assumes. `partykit:::kidids_node()` resolves a missing value by `sample()`ing the split probabilities when no surrogate applies, and `ctree()` stores no surrogates by default, so `predict()` returns a different answer on each call for the same row. There is no deterministic value to match, and the "18/20 differ" counts originally recorded on the issue were measuring a coin flip. Returning `NA` is the honest answer, and keeps the never-drop-rows rule.

Unlike the `randomForest` guard in #329, this propagates per split rather than blanket, so a row only becomes `NA` once its path actually reaches a split on a column it is missing. Blanking a predictor the tree never splits on leaves every prediction unchanged.

The missing check is built from the split's columns rather than its condition, because the two disagree: `NA %in% c("a", "b")` is `FALSE`, not `NA`, so a categorical split would otherwise send a missing value quietly down the right branch.

## Test plan

```r
Rscript -e "devtools::test(filter = '^model-(partykit|cforest|mboost)$')"
```

Also worth checking the SQL, since the new arm has to translate: `tidypredict_sql()` on a `ctree` now emits `WHEN ("wt" IS NULL) THEN NULL` ahead of each split.

title: Return NA for incomplete rows in randomForest and aorsf
description:
Part of #294, and fixes #325. Both backends decline to score a row with a missing predictor: `randomForest::predict()` returns `NA` for it and `aorsf` refuses outright. tidypredict returned a confident value instead, because the generated tree expression routes such a row on whichever comparisons happen not to involve the missing column.

The guard is blanket rather than per split. `randomForest::predict()` returns `NA` whenever *any* predictor is missing, including one the row's path never consults, so testing every predictor is what actually reproduces it. That means the parsed model has to carry the predictor names, since a column used by no split is not otherwise recoverable from the trees.

The remaining models in the #294 matrix need different treatment and are not touched here: `rpart` and `bagger` route missing values through surrogate splits, `ranger` and `cubist` have their own deterministic rules, and the partykit family turns out not to be matchable at all (see below).

## Test plan

Worth knowing while reviewing the rest of #294: `partykit::ctree()` routes a missing value by **random sampling** (`partykit:::kidids_node` falls back to `sample()` on the split probabilities when no surrogate resolves it), so repeated `predict()` calls on the same incomplete row return different values. There is no deterministic prediction for tidypredict to match there, which changes what the fix for `ctree`, `cforest` and `blackboost` can aim for.

```r
Rscript -e "devtools::test(filter = '^model-(rf|aorsf)$')"
```

title: Handle missing predictions and empty data in tidypredict_test()
description:
Fixes #309. `tidypredict_test()` errored with "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" as soon as either side produced an `NA`, because `abs(NA) > threshold` made the `alert` flag itself `NA`. That made it unusable for exactly the case it is most wanted for: checking how a model behaves on missing data, which is what the rest of the #294 work needs. A missing value is now treated as a prediction like any other, so two `NA`s agree and one `NA` against a number is reported as a mismatch, counted separately from a large numeric difference.

Separately, a comparison over zero rows counted zero failures and so reported that all results were within the threshold, while warning from `max(numeric(0))`. That now errors.

title: Fix glm prediction intervals and guard the dbplyr calls
description:
Two unrelated but small user-facing bugs.

`tidypredict_interval()` returned `numeric(0)` for every gaussian `glm()`. The residual variance was read from `summary()$sigma`, which only `summary.lm()` has; `summary.glm()` reports it as `dispersion`. `NULL` then spliced silently into the interval expression, so there was no error or warning, just no rows, and `tidypredict_to_column(add_interval = TRUE)` errored downstream.

`tidypredict_sql()` and `tidypredict_sql_interval()` called `dbplyr::translate_sql()` with no guard and ran `library(dbplyr)` in their examples, which CRAN flags for a Suggests-only package. Both now call `rlang::check_installed("dbplyr")` and use `@examplesIf`. They were also tagged `@keywords internal` despite being exported and advertised in the README, which hid them from the reference index; that tag is gone.

Fixes #293. Fixes #314.

## Test plan

For #293, the existing test only asserted `expect_type(interval, "language")`, which is why this went unnoticed. It now compares against `predict.lm(interval = "prediction")` on the equivalent `lm`, which agrees to ~5e-15, plus a test that `tidypredict_to_column(add_interval = TRUE)` returns a full column.

For #314 I did not add a test: with dbplyr installed the guard cannot fire, and `test-sql.R` already exercises both functions end to end. The change is verified by the examples now running without `library(dbplyr)`.

title: Compare catboost and C5.0 split thresholds as 32-bit floats
description:
Both packages store split thresholds as 32-bit floats and compare them as floats, while tidypredict was reading them into doubles and comparing there. Any value that rounds to the threshold then goes down the wrong branch. `f32_split_boundary()` already existed for exactly this and was already used by Cubist and xgboost; this applies it at the catboost and C5.0 call sites.

Fixes #298. Addresses the float32 item of #287, which bundles three other C5.0 faults not touched here.

## Test plan

Neither defect shows up on ordinary data, which is why the suite was green, so both new tests probe the boundary directly.

**catboost** — every distinct border on one feature, probed a billionth above:

| | Rows disagreeing with `catboost.predict()` |
| --- | --- |
| before | 50 of 52 (max abs diff 1.1) |
| after | 0 of 52 |

**C5.0** — values falling between a cut and its 32-bit float image, swept over 12 datasets x {1, 3} trials x 4 predictors:

| | Rows disagreeing with `predict()` |
| --- | --- |
| before | 40 of 3300 |
| after | 0 of 3300 |

Ordinary (non-boundary) data was unaffected in both cases, before and after.

Two C5.0 snapshots changed, showing cut points at their float boundaries (`cyl <= 6` becomes `cyl <= 6.00000023841858`). That matches how Cubist already renders, e.g. `disp <= 95.1000022888184`.

The last commit adds `catboost_info/` to `.gitignore`; catboost writes it into the working directory whenever the tests train a model.

title: Add tidypredict_save() and tidypredict_load()
description:
The save workflow in `vignette("save")` recommended `yaml::write_yaml()`, which writes numbers with 7 significant digits by default. That is not enough to store a split threshold exactly, so a re-loaded tree model could send rows down a different branch than the model it was saved from, silently. These helpers wrap the write and read so the precision is set correctly, and the vignette now points at them.

One thing worth checking in review: #307 suggested `precision = 17`, but that turns out not to be sufficient. Writing 50,000 doubles and reading them back, `precision = 17` left 1,887 of them altered and `precision = 19` left 338; only 20 and above round trip exactly. (`%.17g` *is* exact in C, so `yaml`'s `precision` argument evidently does not map onto it directly.) The helper uses 22, the largest value `yaml` accepts.

Fixes #307

## Test plan

The new tests in `test-save.R` assert that predictions from a saved-and-reloaded model are identical, not merely close. Verified across six model types before and after:

| Model | Documented workflow | `tidypredict_save()` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ctree` | 200/200 rows differ, max 2.46 | 0 rows differ |
| `cforest` | 200/200 rows differ, max 1.19 | 0 rows differ |
| `rpart` | 200/200 rows differ, max 4.9e-08 | 0 rows differ |
| `ranger` | 200/200 rows differ, max 4.5e-08 | 0 rows differ |
| `randomForest` | 200/200 rows differ, max 3.6e-08 | 0 rows differ |
| `lm` | 200/200 rows differ, max 1.5e-07 | 0 rows differ |

The `ctree` and `cforest` rows are genuine branch flips rather than rounding noise.

`test-model-aorsf.R` had a `tolerance = 1e-6` absorbing this; it now round trips exactly, so the tolerance is gone.

title: Select the longest matching variable name by position, not rank
description:
`parse_label_lm()` picked the longest matching variable name by indexing with `rank()`, which returns ranks rather than positions. With three or more variable names that are prefixes of one another (`x`, `xy`, `xyz`), the wrong variable was selected and the factor level was sliced at the wrong offset, producing silently wrong predictions with no error or warning.

Because the parsing helper is shared, this affected `lm()`, `glm()`, `quantreg::rq()`, `nnet::multinom()`, `nnet::nnet()` and `earth::earth()`. I checked all six against their own `predict()` on the reported data and they now agree to within 2e-15; the existing test for this behaviour only used two nested names, which is why it never caught it.

Fixes #290

title: Document the supported models in one place
description:
The README's "Supported models" list had fallen well behind the dev version, listing 12 model families against 43 supported classes and 9 parsnip engines against roughly 30 (#318). Rather than refresh the list in place and watch it rot again, this adds a `Supported models` article as the single list of record, with the fitted class, parsnip spec and engine, and a link to a worked example for each, and reduces the README to a category summary plus an exact count. The pkgdown articles index gains an explicit `articles:` section too, since a link to a "model list" is only useful if that page isn't a flat dump of every vignette with `save`, `sql` and `float-precision` mixed in among the models.

The one incidental change is in `README.md`: rebuilding it picked up the current `simulate_mssql()` output (`[wt]` rather than `` `wt` ``), which the committed copy predated.

## Test plan

`pkgdown::check_pkgdown()` and a site build could not run locally (`tidytemplate` would not install), so the `articles:` section was verified by diffing its contents against `vignettes/*.Rmd`: all 35 vignettes listed exactly once, nothing phantom. Worth a real `pkgdown::build_site()` to confirm the grouped index and the new article's relative links resolve.

title: Normalise the test suite conventions
description:
Phase 3 item 3.8, the style sweep. Five mechanical commits, no production code touched.

The substantive one is the third: 61 tests wrapped `tidypredict_test()` in `expect_snapshot()`, which turns a numeric regression into a snapshot diff rather than a failure. They now assert on `$alert`, as `CONTRIBUTING.md` asks. That also revealed two warnings the snapshots had been swallowing, from deliberately degenerate glm and rq fits; both are suppressed explicitly at the call site with a note, so the suite's warning count is unchanged rather than quietly higher.

The rest: `withr::local_tempfile()` in the 20 files that leaked temp files, `skip_if_not_installed()` in the four files that had no installed-check for their own suggested package, and the drifted test descriptions.

Two things in the plan's list are deliberately not here:

- **The `round_print()` sweep.** It would rewrite snapshot content across 22 files, and the plan asks for every snapshot diff to be reviewed by hand rather than blanket-accepted. Twenty-two files of numeric churn cannot be meaningfully hand-verified, so the sweep would mean accepting on faith in exactly the place a real change could hide. The fragility it guards against is also still hypothetical: no snapshot has actually broken on precision. `test-model-glm.R`'s two different ad hoc roundings fall under the same heading and are likewise untouched.
- **The 27 copies of `"returns the right output"`.** Uninformative rather than inconsistent. Naming each one meaningfully is a judgment call per test, not a sweep.

No snapshot keys moved, incidentally: none of the renamed tests take snapshots, because the save-and-reload tests assert on predictions and the agreement tests were converted in the preceding commit.

Suite is 1770 passing, unchanged, and `R CMD check` is clean.

title: Fill out the thin test files and pin the version 3 format
description:
Phase 3 items 3.4 and 3.6, applying the battery from #279 to the four thinnest model test files and adding version 3 fixtures. Doing so uncovered two real prediction bugs, both of which had gone unnoticed for the same reason: the tree family had no per-model round-trip test, which is exactly the gap the plan predicted after 1c.

**Cubist sent rows on a split boundary down the wrong branch.** Cubist stores thresholds as 32-bit floats and compares as floats, so a `disp` of exactly 95.1 belongs on the `<=` side of a threshold stored as 95.099998. In doubles it went the other way, making the Lotus Europa's prediction 6.2 off. This is the mirror image of the xgboost bug from #273, which needed the threshold nudged toward the next *lower* float because its comparison is `<`, so the two helpers now live in `R/float32.R` behind a `side` argument.

**randomForest parsed models split on the wrong columns.** Leaves report a split variable of 0, and indexing the term labels with a 0 drops the element instead of yielding `NA`. `ifelse()` then read that shortened vector at the original positions, so every split name after the first leaf in a tree was wrong. Reloaded models were off by up to 2.4 on mtcars. Only the parsed path was affected, since the direct builder indexes one node at a time with a non-zero variable.

The v3 fixtures are built differently from the existing v2 ones: each stores the predictions the modelling package itself produced when the fixture was generated. The tests therefore compare against ground truth rather than another tidypredict result, and they run without the modelling packages installed. One of them asserts that the fixtures carry no `pm_tree_*` class, which is the property #277 relies on when it derives that class at read time.

## Test plan

Two changes to existing tests were forced rather than chosen, and both are the antipattern the battery warns about:

- `test-model-cubist.R`'s reload test compared two tidypredict formulas as text. The corrected Cubist threshold does not survive a YAML round-trip byte for byte, so it now compares predictions against Cubist's own `predict()` with a tolerance.
- The rq YAML round-trip needs `tolerance = 1e-6` because YAML stores fewer digits than a double carries. Worth knowing when writing the next one.

Suite is 1770 passing. One `R CMD check` run reported a test failure with 85 skips against the usual 0, meaning that run saw an incomplete package library; it does not reproduce, and repeat runs are 0/0/0.

title: Write down the test battery and close the load-bearing coverage gaps
description:
Phase 3 items 3.2, 3.3 and 3.5. The battery is now written down in `CONTRIBUTING.md`, with `CLAUDE.md` pointing at it so both humans and agent-driven work share one source.

Writing the missing tests turned up three real bugs, which is the point of the exercise:

- **`tidypredict_interval()` ignored its `interval` argument.** `te_interval_lm()` hardcoded `0.95` in its `qt()` call while accepting an `interval` parameter, and `tidypredict_interval.list()` never forwarded the argument at all. Asking for a 99% interval returned a 95% one, through `tidypredict_interval()`, `tidypredict_to_column(add_interval = TRUE)`, and `tidypredict_sql_interval()` alike.
- **`tidypredict_to_column()` blamed the wrong thing.** Its error said tree based models are unsupported, but the condition it guards is a model returning more than one formula, which is the multiclass and multivariate case. Trees work fine.
- **No `tidypredict_test()` method for C5.0**, which is why that file had no numeric agreement test against C5.0's own `predict()`.

The first two were found by `test-predict-column.R`, which is the first real test of `tidypredict_to_column()`. Before this it was called exactly once in the entire suite and mocked everywhere else, despite `tidypredict_test()` being built on top of it.

I also added `tidypredict_interval.default()` so an unsupported class names itself rather than producing R's "no applicable method" error, matching what #277 did for `tidypredict_fit()`.

One plan item needed no work: the catboost `as_parsed_model` round-trip already exists at `test-model-catboost.R:1024`, including a comparison against native `predict()`. The plan's note that it was missing was stale.

## Test plan

The C5.0 tests include one assertion that looks redundant and is not: it checks that `result$raw_results$fit` really comes from `predict(model, iris)`. A `tidypredict_test()` method whose two sides both originate from tidypredict can never set `alert`, which is exactly how ranger's method was broken, and a passing suite cannot distinguish the two situations.

Suite is 1724 passing. `R CMD check` is clean; `CONTRIBUTING.md` is added to `.Rbuildignore` to keep it that way.

title: Remove dead branches and strengthen the round-trip tests
description:
Closes out the cleanup items: the unreachable length-1 guard around `reduce_or()`, and four `_snaps/<version>/` directories left over from a run that set a snapshot variant. Nothing in the suite sets `variant` any more, so testthat never reads them, and their contents still record the flat `case_when` format that version 3 replaced. Per your call, the legacy ranger tree walkers stay.

The more useful half is the round-trip audit. Three tests (C5.0 twice, catboost, lightgbm) compared a serialized parsed model against the un-serialized one, which only proves serialization is lossless: a parser that is wrong the same way on both sides passes happily. They now compare against the model's own `predict()`.

I left the `tidypredict_fit(model)` versus `tidypredict_fit(pm)` comparisons in the other ten or so files alone. Those check the direct path against the parsed path, which is a real assertion rather than a self-comparison, and every one of those files already has a separate test against `predict()`.

Also corrects the header comment in the xgboost tests, which claimed `mtcars[, -9]` avoids split boundaries. It does not, and that is exactly what the f32 tests in the same file exist to cover.

title: Replace the structural duplication in the model builders
description:
This is the structural half of the deduplication pass, following #274 through #276. Six changes, one commit each, ordered from lowest to highest risk so a regression is easy to attribute.

The two that change behaviour rather than just shape are worth a reviewer's attention. `tidypredict_fit()` gains a `default` method, replacing fifteen methods that did nothing but parse and delegate; it checks for a `parse_model()` method first, so an unsupported class now names the class instead of producing R's "no applicable method" error. And `tidypredict_fit.pm_tree()` stops comparing `model$general$model` against eight strings, dispatching on a class instead. That class is derived at dispatch time rather than stored by `as_parsed_model()`, specifically so that parsed models serialized before this change still find their builder.

I left the planned `expr_affine()` out. The scale-and-bias sites in catboost, mboost, bart and h2o each order their arithmetic differently and skip identity terms under different conditions, so sharing a spelling would churn generated SQL without removing any real logic.

## Test plan

Two snags are worth knowing about, since both are invisible in the diff:

- `multinom` objects also inherit from `nnet`, so `tidypredict_fit.multinom()` cannot fall through to the new default; it would reach the nnet method. It is kept, with a comment saying why. Eight nnet tests caught this.
- The `build_tree_formula` methods are written as full function definitions rather than assigned aliases, because R collates `R/` alphabetically and `predict-fit.R` loads after every `model-*.R`.

Four lightgbm snapshots record an internal function name in an error message and now read `assemble_lgb_formula()`; the messages themselves are unchanged.

Suite is 1696 passing, and `R CMD check` is clean. Note that re-building `vignettes/h2o.Rmd` needs a live h2o cluster and fails intermittently regardless of these changes.

title: Share one expression for the logistic inverse link
description:
Seven places mapped a linear predictor onto a probability, and they had drifted into two different spellings of the same function. That turned out to matter rather than being cosmetic: the minority spelling, `1 - 1 / (1 + exp(f))`, cancels catastrophically and returns exactly 0 once the linear predictor drops below about -37, so `glm(family = binomial)` and `LiblineaR` silently lost every small probability. This unifies all seven on `1 / (1 + exp(-f))`, which is accurate across the whole range.

One snapshot changed, and only because it happened to record the formula as text; the numbers it stood for are unaffected except where they were previously wrong.

title: Share the helpers duplicated across model files
description:
Adding each new model by copying an existing `model-*.R` left several families of byte-identical helpers behind. This removes eight of them, cutting about 440 lines. It is purely internal: no snapshot changed anywhere in the suite, and there are no `NEWS.md` bullets as a result.

The extractions are `build_terms()` for nine copies of the parsed-model term builder, `parsnip_vars()` for three, `expr_softmax()` for six, `expr_mean()` for eight, `build_argmax_case_when()` for three, `new_multiclass_parsed_model()` for seven, and two abort helpers replacing eight and twelve copies respectively. `build_terms()` reaches past the six identical copies into lm and glmnet, which had the same shape with an extra QR field and a zero-coefficient filter.

Two groups I had originally listed are deliberately left out. The tree parsed-model skeletons share only three lines before their tails diverge, one of which puts fields under `$general` and another at the top level, so a shared constructor would need a flexible-field API costing more than it saves. The `acceptable_formula` methods are already one-line delegations, so consolidating them means relocating six definitions with no reduction, and it would work against keeping each model's methods beside the rest of its code.

## Test plan

The useful check here is that nothing moved: `devtools::test()` passes with no accepted snapshots. Two changes were only caught because of that, and both are worth a glance in the diff. `expr_mean()` takes the tree count as an argument because the forests read it off the model as a double while other callers use `length()`, and passing it keeps rf and ranger writing `/3` rather than `/3L`. `abort_test_unsupported()` runs `cli::format_inline()` over its `what` argument, because cli does not re-parse markup inside an interpolated value and the messages would otherwise print literal braces.

Unrelated to this branch: the h2o tests failed twice during full-suite runs and passed in isolation both times, which is cluster state from an old local h2o rather than anything here.

title: Share the result assembly across tidypredict_test methods
description:
Every `tidypredict_test()` method obtained the model's own predictions, obtained tidypredict's, and compared them, but only the first two steps genuinely differ between models. The comparison, message and returned object were copied sixteen times, which is how the threshold and message bugs fixed in #273 stayed hidden for so long. This collects them into `R/test-results.R`, removing about 740 lines across ten files.

There are three comparison shapes rather than one (numeric with optional intervals, exact class matching, and a matrix of class probabilities), so each gets its own assembler over a shared constructor instead of one helper with mode flags. The methods themselves stay in their model files.

Consolidating forced three inconsistencies in `raw_results` to be resolved, so this is not purely internal. The model's own prediction was called `base` for XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost and h2o and `fit` everywhere else, and `fit` now wins. `fit_diff` was signed in eleven methods and already absolute in three, and is now signed throughout with the threshold applied to its absolute value. Classification results were built two different ways, one of which printed a meaningless "Max difference: 1" for a class label, and now share one shape.

Worth a close look: the ranger commit is a real bug fix, not cleanup. `predict.ranger()` returns a list rather than a vector, so the old code built a column named `prediction` and `raw_results$fit` then partial-matched `fit_te`. The difference was `fit_te - fit_te`, so ranger's numeric-agreement test was comparing tidypredict against itself and could never fail. Its recorded snapshot has been a tautology.

## Test plan

The snapshot changes are all intentional and each was checked rather than accepted wholesale: the default method's max-difference label gains consistent spacing, glmnet no longer reports a negative maximum, and three C5.0 classification tests now report `Difference threshold: 0` instead of the `1e-12` default argument that was accepted and then ignored.

`tests/testthat/test-test-results.R` covers the extracted helpers directly, including a negative difference that the previous signed comparison would have missed. That case could not be tested before, because the logic was inlined in every method.

title: Fix xgboost predictions and tidypredict_test threshold reporting
description:
Reviewing the recently added model support turned up three defects in xgboost prediction and `tidypredict_test()` reporting, all of which were invisible because the tests that should have caught them compared tidypredict's output against itself rather than against the model's own `predict()`. The first commit adds the regression tests and fails; the rest fix the bugs.

The two prediction bugs are worth a look in the diff. xgboost compares split thresholds as 32-bit floats, so any feature value landing exactly on a threshold was routed down the wrong branch; thresholds are now shifted to the midpoint between the float and its predecessor so the comparison in doubles is exactly equivalent. Separately, reconstructing a tree from a saved parsed model collapsed it to a single leaf, because xgboost stores leaf paths root-last while lightgbm stores them root-first and the shared reconstruction assumed the latter.

`fit_diff` still means a signed difference in eleven `tidypredict_test()` methods and an absolute one in three. That inconsistency is untouched here and is better resolved alongside deduplicating these sixteen near-identical methods.

## Test plan

The first commit is expected to fail on its own; the branch is green as a whole. To confirm the prediction fixes actually agree with xgboost rather than just with each other:

```r
devtools::test(filter = "^model-(xgboost|lightgbm|catboost)$")
```

Verified separately across tree depths 1 to 6, three objectives, and data containing `NA`, where parsed and direct predictions now agree exactly.

title: Support MASS qda models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `MASS::qda()`, including `discrim_quad()` parsnip models fitted with the `"MASS"` engine. Each class score is expanded from the per-class covariance into a quadratic polynomial (intercept, one coefficient per predictor, one per predictor pair), which lets the parsed model reuse the existing linear-term structure and softmax builder shared with `MASS::lda()`. `tidypredict_fit()` returns a named list of class-probability expressions, so `tidypredict_test()` is not supported.

Part of #232.

title: Support C5.0 base models in bagger ensembles
description:
Extends the `baguette::bagger()` support added in #269 to the `"C5.0"` base model, so `bag_tree()` models fit with the `"C5.0"` engine work too. Classification predictions average the per-tree class probabilities, which C5.0 reports at a leaf as `(freq + prior) / (n_leaf + 1)` using the class proportions of the training sample.

Getting there also required teaching the C5.0 parser about discrete splits that use one branch per level (node type 1), which it previously rejected outright. That affects plain `C5.0()` models as well, and any bagged model with a factor predictor hit it immediately.

One pre-existing limitation this surfaced but does not fix: C5.0 writes cut points into its text tree at ~8 significant digits and compares data as C `float`, so a value within ~1e-7 relative of a cut can fall on the wrong side of the generated `<=`. Worth a follow-up if we want a relative-epsilon nudge on the thresholds.

Part of #232.

title: Support baguette bagger models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `baguette::bagger()` ensembles fit with the `"CART"` base model, which also covers `bag_tree()` parsnip models fitted with the `"rpart"` engine. Regression predictions average the individual trees; classification averages the per-tree class probabilities and returns the class with the largest average, matching how baguette breaks ties.

Getting the classification probabilities to line up with `predict()` surfaced a bug in the existing rpart support: rpart sends values strictly below a cut point to the left child, but the generated `case_when()` used `<=`. That is invisible for a single tree whose cut points are midpoints between observed values, and routinely wrong for trees fit on bootstrap samples of the data being predicted. Continuous rpart splits now emit `<`, which changes the `model-rpart` snapshot.

title: Support dbarts bart models
description:
Adds support for `dbarts::bart()` Bayesian additive regression trees, including `bart()` parsnip models fitted with the `"dbarts"` engine, so BART predictions can run in the database. Only continuous outcomes are supported: binary outcomes are fit with a probit link, whose `pnorm()` has no SQL translation, and the model has to be fit with `keeptrees = TRUE` since the trees are otherwise discarded. Both cases error with an explanation.

One thing worth knowing while reviewing: parsnip's `predict()` for `bart()` draws from the posterior *predictive* distribution, which adds residual noise, so it only agrees with `tidypredict_fit()` in expectation. The parsnip test compares against `predict(model$fit, df, type = "ev")` instead.

title: Support nnet neural network models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `nnet::nnet()` single hidden layer neural networks, which is what `mlp()` fits with the `"nnet"` engine, for both regression and classification. Classification models return a named list of class-probability expressions, so `tidypredict_test()` is not supported for them.

Two things a reviewer might otherwise wonder about. The generated expressions replicate the hard saturation of the squashing function of nnet (exactly 0 below -15, exactly 1 above 15) rather than emitting a plain logistic; without it predictions drift from `predict()` by up to ~3e-7, well past the 1e-12 threshold of `tidypredict_test()`. And parsnip runs the probabilities that `predict.nnet()` has already normalized through a second softmax, so the `model_fit` path mirrors that in order to match `predict(model, type = "prob")`.

Part of #232.

title: Support naivebayes naive_bayes models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `naivebayes::naive_bayes()`, alongside the existing `klaR::NaiveBayes()` support, so `naive_Bayes()` models fitted with the `"naivebayes"` engine can be turned into class-probability expressions. All four non-kernel conditional distributions are covered (Gaussian, Categorical, Bernoulli, Poisson); `usekernel = TRUE` fits are rejected since kernel densities can't be expressed as a Tidy Eval formula.

Poisson terms drop the `log(x!)` factor, which is safe because it does not depend on the class and cancels in the softmax normalization. This checks off `naivebayes::naive_bayes()` in #232.

## Test plan

The vignette cannot be rendered against the installed tidypredict until this and #264 are installed, so the new `naivebayes` section was verified with `devtools::load_all()` rather than `rmarkdown::render()`. Worth a second look after install.

title: Support klaR NaiveBayes models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `klaR::NaiveBayes()` classifiers fit with Gaussian densities, including `naive_Bayes()` parsnip models on the `"klaR"` engine. Since predicting normalizes a product of a prior and one conditional density per predictor, the posterior probabilities are the softmax of the summed log densities, which is what `tidypredict_fit()` emits: one expression per outcome class. Kernel density fits (`usekernel = TRUE`) are rejected because those densities cannot be translated.

Part of #232.

title: Support parsnip nullmodel models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `parsnip::nullmodel()`, the fitted object behind `null_model()`, so the baseline model can be scored alongside every other supported model type. Since a null model ignores its predictors, regression parses to a single intercept term holding the outcome mean (reusing the existing linear path) and classification returns one constant class-probability expression per level.

Part of #232.

title: Support mixOmics PLS models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for the partial least squares models in mixOmics (`pls()`, `spls()`, `plsda()`, `splsda()`), including `pls()` parsnip models fitted with the `"mixOmics"` engine, checking off another box in #232. Because `predict.mixo_pls()` collapses all components into a single coefficient matrix, prediction folds down to a plain linear combination once the centering and scaling are absorbed into the coefficients, so these reuse the existing linear and multinomial formula builders.

Worth flagging for the reviewer: mixOmics is a Bioconductor package and the first Bioc dependency here, so DESCRIPTION probably needs a `biocViews:` field for `R CMD check` to resolve it from Suggests. I left that out as a packaging policy call. Separately, `plsmod` derives hard class labels from Mahalanobis distance in component space rather than from these probabilities, so `argmax` over the returned class expressions will not always match `predict(type = "class")`; the probabilities themselves are exact.

title: Support sparsediscrim discriminant analysis models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for the regularized linear discriminant analysis models in `sparsediscrim` (`lda_diag()`, `lda_shrink_mean()`, `lda_shrink_cov()`, and `lda_emp_bayes_eigen()`), which are the models behind the `"sparsediscrim"` engine of `discrim_linear()`. All four share a per-class mean and prior plus a single pooled covariance, so their posteriors reduce to a softmax over one linear predictor per class and reuse the existing multinomial machinery. Part of #232.

One thing worth knowing while reviewing: `predict(type = "prob")` is unusable upstream for `lda_emp_bayes_eigen()` (`regularization_method = "min_distance"`), because sparsediscrim builds a rank-deficient pooled covariance and returns `NaN` for every row. The generated expressions instead use the model's own pseudo-inverse of that covariance, so that method is tested against `predict(type = "class")` rather than against native probabilities.

title: Support sda discriminant analysis models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `sda::sda()` shrinkage discriminant analysis models, including `discrim_linear()` parsnip models fitted with the `"sda"` engine. Part of #232.

`predict.sda()` is already a softmax over `X %*% t(beta) + alpha`, so the parser reuses the existing multiclass builder. One wrinkle worth knowing about while reviewing: `sda()` is fit from a numeric matrix and keeps no formula, so a directly fitted model can only name the matrix columns it was given. The `model_fit` path therefore passes the parsnip formula down so dummy columns like `gear4` become conditionals on the original factor. Tests compare against `predict()` at `1e-6` because `sda()` runs its posteriors through `zapsmall()`.

title: Support mda fda models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `mda::fda()` flexible discriminant analysis models, including `discrim_linear()` parsnip models fitted with the `"mda"` engine. Part of #232.

Support is limited to fits whose inner regression is linear in the predictors (`mda::polyreg()` at `degree = 1` and `mda::gen.ridge()`); with that restriction the posterior probabilities collapse into a softmax over per-class linear predictors, so the parser can reuse the existing multiclass builder. `mda::mars()`, `mda::bruto()`, higher polynomial degrees, and the mixture models from `mda::mda()` error with an explanatory message.

title: Support MASS lda models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `MASS::lda()` linear discriminant analysis models, including `discrim_linear()` parsnip models fitted with the `"MASS"` engine. Part of #232.

`predict.lda()` centers the model matrix at the prior-weighted grand mean, projects it onto the discriminant space, and compares the result to each class centroid. That path is linear in the predictors, so it collapses into one coefficient vector plus intercept per class and the posteriors are the softmax of those linear predictors, which lets the parser reuse the existing multiclass softmax builder rather than introduce a new one.

title: Add support for H2O RuleFit models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `h2o::h2o.rulefit()` models, reachable through the `"h2o"` engine of `rule_fit()`. A RuleFit model is a lasso over rule indicators plus linear terms, all of which H2O exposes through `h2o.rule_importance()`, so the rules are read from there rather than walked tree-by-tree the way the existing H2O GBM support does.

Regression and binary classification are supported. Multiclass models deliberately error instead: comparing `h2o.rule_importance()` against the underlying GLM shows it reports only a subset of the non-zero coefficients for multinomial fits and misattributes others (rules whose coefficients tie across classes get collapsed into a single row), so the per-class linear predictors are not recoverable. Three-class fits happened to reconstruct exactly in every trial, but four- and six-class fits were reliably wrong, and silently incorrect predictions seemed worse than an explicit error.

## Test plan

The tests need a running H2O cluster and skip without one, so they will not exercise this in CI. Locally, with Java available:

```
Rscript -e "devtools::test(filter = '^h2o')"
Rscript -e "devtools::test(filter = '^tidymodels')"
```

Correctness was checked beyond the committed tests by refitting across seeds, `model_type`, `lambda`, and rule-length settings and comparing `tidypredict_test()` against `h2o.predict()` (max difference ~1e-14). Worth eyeballing the new RuleFit section of `vignettes/h2o.Rmd`, which renders against a live cluster.

title: Add support for xrf RuleFit models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `xrf::xrf()` RuleFit models, including `rule_fit()` parsnip models fitted with the `"xrf"` engine, covering regression and binary classification. Part of #232.

An xrf model is a lasso fit over raw columns plus rule indicators, so it reuses the existing linear formula builder: each rule becomes a product of indicator terms, and splits on one-hot dummy columns are translated back onto the original factor column (`cyl8 >= 0.5` becomes `cyl == "8"`) so the formula only references columns that exist in the data.

title: Support nnet multinom_reg models
description: Adds tidypredict support for `nnet::multinom()` multinomial log-linear models, including `multinom_reg()` parsnip models fitted with the `"nnet"` engine. Like the recently added multinomial glmnet support, `tidypredict_fit()` returns a named list of softmax class-probability expressions (with the first outcome level as the reference class), and `tidypredict_test()` is not supported for these multiclass models. Part of #232.

title: Support multinomial glmnet models (#198)
description: Adds tidypredict support for multinomial `glmnet::glmnet()` models (`family = "multinomial"`), which is what `multinom_reg()` fitted with the `"glmnet"` engine produces. Because these models are multiclass, `tidypredict_fit()` returns a named list of class-probability expressions (one softmax expression per outcome level) rather than a single expression, mirroring how the multiclass boosting models already behave; `tidypredict_test()` errors for them since there is no single-column prediction to compare against.

title: Support LiblineaR SVM regression and classification models
description:
tidypredict already parsed `LiblineaR::LiblineaR()` logistic regression models but rejected the SVM `type` codes that parsnip's `svm_linear()` engine produces, so `svm_linear()` LiblineaR fits could not be translated. This extends the parser to also handle support-vector regression (`type` 11-13) and binary SVM classification (`type` 1-5).

Because LiblineaR SVM classifiers expose no probabilities, classification returns the raw SVM decision value (oriented to the first class) rather than a probability, matching `predict(..., decisionValues = TRUE)`.

title: Add support for kernlab linear SVM models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `kernlab::ksvm()` models fit with the linear (`vanilladot`) kernel, including `svm_linear()` parsnip models using the `"kernlab"` engine, for regression and binary classification. With a linear kernel the decision function collapses to a weighted sum of the predictors, so both modes reuse the existing linear-model formula builder after undoing kernlab's internal scaling; binary classification folds kernlab's Platt-scaling probability into the glm logit path and predicts the second factor level to match the existing glm/LiblineaR convention.

Non-linear kernels and multiclass classification are not supported, and classification requires a probability model (`prob.model = TRUE`), since one-vs-one voting can't be expressed as a single linear formula. (#232)

title: Add support for rule-based C5.0 models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for rule-based C5.0 models (`rules = TRUE`), including `C5_rules()` parsnip models fitted with the `"C5.0"` engine, which were previously rejected. A case's prediction sums each satisfied rule's confidence-weighted vote per class and returns the class with the greatest total, with the default class winning ties and unmatched cases, reproducing C5.0's own `RuleClassify`/`SelectClass`. Boosted rule sets (`trials > 1`) are not supported and raise an informative error.

## Test plan

`Rscript -e "devtools::test_active_file('R/model-C5.0.R')"` and `Rscript -e "devtools::test_active_file('R/tidymodels.R')"`. The correctness tests evaluate the generated formula and compare it against `predict()` on numeric, categorical, and multiclass fits (including the mixed-type `attrition` dataset, which exercises all three C5.0 rule condition kinds).

title: Add H2O GBM support for boost_tree()
description:
This adds tidypredict support for H2O gradient boosting models (`H2ORegressionModel`, `H2OBinomialModel`, `H2OMultinomialModel`), including `boost_tree()` parsnip models fitted with agua's `"h2o_gbm"` engine, for both regression and classification. Trees are pulled from the running H2O cluster and turned into nested `case_when()` expressions, so a live `h2o.init()` connection is required to build or evaluate a formula. Scope is limited to H2O's GBM (not its XGBoost) and the gaussian, bernoulli, and multinomial distributions. Addresses part of #232.

## Test plan

H2O tests require a running cluster and are skipped otherwise. To run them locally with a cluster available: `Rscript -e "devtools::test(filter = '^h2o')"` and `Rscript -e "devtools::test(filter = '^tidymodels')"`.

title: Add tidypredict support for mboost blackboost models
description:
Adds support for `mboost::blackboost()` gradient boosting regression models, checking off the `boost_tree()` / mboost item in #232. Prediction is reconstructed as `offset + nu * (sum of per-tree terminal-node values)`, which matches native `predict()` to machine precision. Only the Gaussian family is supported; other families apply a non-linear response function and are rejected with a clear error.

parsnip does not currently ship an `"mboost"` engine for `boost_tree()`, so there is no parsnip path to test yet, but the existing `model_fit` delegation will pick up blackboost automatically once such an engine is registered.

title: Support boosted C5.0 models and the boost_tree() C5.0 engine
description:
Adds tidypredict support for boosted `C50::C5.0()` classification models, which previously errored, and wires up `boost_tree()` parsnip models fitted with the `"C5.0"` engine. Boosting combines its trials by confidence-weighted voting (each trial votes for its predicted class weighted by that leaf's Laplace-ratio confidence, and the class with the greatest total vote wins), reproduced here as a nested `case_when()` cascade over the summed per-class votes. This checks the `boost_tree()` + C5.0 box in #232.

While auditing the `C5.0()`/`C5.0Control()` options, I found two that change prediction in ways a hard-split `case_when()` cannot reproduce: `fuzzyThreshold = TRUE` (soft splits that route cases fractionally down both branches, which was silently giving wrong answers in the existing single-tree support) and `costs` (a cost matrix that alters class selection). Both now raise a clear error, alongside the existing `rules = TRUE` guard.

title: Add support for aorsf oblique random forest models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `aorsf::orsf()` oblique random forest regression models, including `rand_forest()` parsnip models fitted with the `"aorsf"` engine via bonsai. Unlike axis-aligned forests, each split is a linear combination of standardized predictors; the forest's stored centering and scaling are folded into the split coefficients so the generated formula works on the raw columns. Only regression with numeric predictors is supported, matching how the existing forest engines handle classification.

One caveat worth flagging: aorsf uses observed linear-combination values as split cutpoints, so a training row can land exactly on a boundary where floating-point drift flips a branch. Agreement with `predict()` is exact on new data, so the tests exercise jittered data and the caveat is documented in the vignette.

title: Add support for partykit cforest random forest models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `partykit::cforest()` regression models, including `rand_forest()` parsnip models fitted with the `"partykit"` engine (via bonsai). This fills in another entry on the supported model types and engines checklist (#232).

The one non-obvious piece worth a reviewer's attention: cforest prediction is not a simple average of per-tree node means. With partykit's default `scale = TRUE`, `predict()` averages each tree's in-bag *weighted* terminal-node mean, so the node predictions are weighted by the in-bag sampling weights before the trees are combined. Classification is not supported, matching the existing ranger and randomForest engines.

title: Add support for C5.0 decision tree models
description:
Adds tidypredict support for `C50::C5.0()` classification trees, including `decision_tree()` parsnip models fitted with the `"C5.0"` engine. The parser reads the tree structure C5.0 serializes as text rather than converting through `partykit::as.party()`, since that conversion re-evaluates the fitting call to recover the training data, which is unavailable when the model is fit through the x/y interface (as parsnip does). Boosted (`trials > 1`) and rule-based (`rules = TRUE`) models are not representable as a single tree and raise an error.

Relates to #232; the `decision_tree()`/C5.0 checkbox can be checked there.

title: Add rpart engine support for decision_tree() parsnip models
description: The `rpart` fitted class was already parsed by tidypredict, so `decision_tree()` parsnip models using the `"rpart"` engine work through delegation with no code changes. This adds a dedicated test covering both regression and classification modes (asserting `tidypredict_fit()`, `tidypredict_sql()`, and `tidypredict_test()`) plus a NEWS entry to make the support explicit.

title: Add support for LiblineaR binary logistic regression models
description: Adds tidypredict support for binary logistic regression models fitted with `LiblineaR::LiblineaR()`, including `logistic_reg()` parsnip models using the `"LiblineaR"` engine (tidymodels/tidypredict#232). The parser reuses the existing linear-model machinery with a logit link, so the fit expression, SQL translation, and orbital paths all work, and predictions follow the glm convention of returning the probability of the second factor level. Multiclass models are out of scope and raise a clear error.

title: add new skills
description: these claude skills aims to aid the addition of new models

title: Add support for quantreg rq quantile regression models
description: Adds `tidypredict` support for quantile regression models fitted with `quantreg::rq()`, addressing the remaining `linear_reg()` engine (`quantreg`) in #232. An `rq` object is a linear model, so the existing `lm` parsing machinery is reused; prediction is supported but intervals are not, since `rq` objects carry no QR decomposition.

title: Make glmnet tests robust and regenerate docs
description: Two small maintenance changes. The glmnet snapshot tests now use `round_print()` so they no longer break on last-digit floating-point differences between glmnet versions, and the Cox family test passes `cox.ties = "breslow"` to silence the glmnet 5.1 deprecation warning. Separately, the package docs are regenerated under roxygen2 8.0.0, which cleans up the internal `generate_nested_case_when_tree` topic and refreshes the reexport and package man pages.

title: Add support for linear_reg() with the glm engine
description: Adds official support and coverage for `linear_reg()` parsnip models fitted with the `"glm"` engine (#232). This already worked at runtime because parsnip's `model_fit` dispatches to the underlying `glm` fit object, so this change makes it tested and documented.

title: speed up the model code
description:
## Results

### ranger

**Issue 1: Data frame row subsetting in recursive function**

The original code in `build_nested_ranger_node()` used `tree[tree$nodeID == node_id, ]` on every recursive call, which is O(n) per node.

**Fix:** Pre-extract all columns as vectors before recursion and use direct vector indexing.

| Configuration | Before | After Round 1 | Speedup |
|---------------|--------|---------------|---------|
| max.depth=10  | 2.15s  | 0.45s         | **4.8x** |
| max.depth=20  | 7.75s  | 2.57s         | **3.0x** |
| num.trees=500 | 10.72s | 2.45s         | **4.4x** |
| num.trees=1000| 22.20s | 5.05s         | **4.4x** |

**Issue 2: Named vector lookup with `as.character()` conversion**

After round 1, profiling showed 55% of time spent on `id_to_idx[[as.character(node_id)]]` - the `as.character()` call on every recursive iteration was expensive.

**Fix:** Since ranger nodeIDs are 0-indexed and sequential, use direct integer indexing `node_id + 1L` instead of named lookup.

| Configuration | After Round 1 | After Round 2 | Speedup |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------|
| max.depth=10  | 0.45s         | 0.17s         | **2.6x** |
| max.depth=20  | 2.57s         | 0.44s         | **5.8x** |
| num.trees=500 | 2.45s         | 0.92s         | **2.7x** |
| num.trees=1000| 5.05s         | 1.88s         | **2.7x** |

**Total improvement:**

| Configuration | Original | Final | Total Speedup |
|---------------|----------|-------|---------------|
| max.depth=10  | 2.15s    | 0.17s | **12.6x** |
| max.depth=20  | 7.75s    | 0.44s | **17.6x** |
| num.trees=500 | 10.72s   | 0.92s | **11.7x** |
| num.trees=1000| 22.20s   | 1.88s | **11.8x** |

**Final profile breakdown (500 trees, depth=10):**
- 26% GC (garbage collection from expression building)
- 21% enexpr (rlang expression building)
- 7% rlang::sym (symbol creation)
- Remaining time distributed across inherent operations

No further obvious optimizations - remaining time is inherent to rlang expression building.

---

### lightgbm

**Issue 1: Duplicate JSON parsing**

The original code parsed `model$dump_model()` via `jsonlite::fromJSON()` twice: once in `parse_model.lgb.Booster()` and again in `extract_lgb_trees_nested()`. JSON parsing took 57% of total time.

**Fix:** Pass `feature_names` from `parsedmodel` to `extract_lgb_trees_nested()` to avoid redundant JSON parsing.

**Issue 2: Slow `grepl()` for string matching**

The `parse_lgb_linear_trees()` function used `grepl("^prefix", line)` in a loop over every line of the model string.

**Fix:** Replace `grepl("^prefix", ...)` with `startsWith(line, "prefix")` which is faster for prefix matching.

**Issue 3: Data frame column access in path building**

The `get_lgb_path()` function used `which(tree_df$split_index == current_parent_split)` (O(n) per iteration) and repeated `tree_df$column[[parent_row]]` access.

**Fix:** Pre-extract columns as vectors and build a split_index to row lookup array for O(1) access.

| Configuration | Before | After | Speedup |
|---------------|--------|-------|---------|
| nrounds=100   | 1.05s  | 0.62s | **1.7x** |
| nrounds=250   | 2.69s  | 1.71s | **1.6x** |
| nrounds=500   | 5.75s  | 3.71s | **1.5x** |

---

### randomForest

**Issue: Matrix row access and repeated `unname()` calls**

The original code used `tree[node_id, ]` to get a row, then called `unname()` on each column value (4-5 times per internal node). This caused:
- 23.8% of time in `unname()` calls
- 128 MB memory allocation from `unname()` alone

**Fix:** Pre-extract all matrix columns as vectors with `unname()` called once per column, then use direct integer indexing.

| Configuration | Before | After | Speedup |
|---------------|--------|-------|---------|
| ntree=100     | 0.96s  | 0.56s | **1.7x** |
| ntree=250     | 2.73s  | 1.55s | **1.8x** |
| ntree=500     | 5.80s  | 3.42s | **1.7x** |

**Final profile breakdown (500 trees):**
- 34% GC (garbage collection from expression building)
- 21% enexpr (rlang expression building)
- 5% rlang::sym (symbol creation)
- Remaining time distributed across inherent operations

No further obvious optimizations - remaining time is inherent to rlang expression building.

---

### catboost

**Issue: Repeated feature info lookups in oblivious tree parsing**

For oblivious trees (same splits for all leaves), the original code parsed each split separately for every leaf. With depth=6 (64 leaves), each of the 6 splits was looked up 64 times per tree instead of once.

**Fix:** Pre-extract split info once per tree, then for each leaf only determine the direction (op) based on bit value.

| Configuration | Before | After | Speedup |
|---------------|--------|-------|---------|
| iterations=100 | 0.18s | 0.15s | **1.2x** |
| iterations=250 | 0.48s | 0.42s | **1.1x** |
| iterations=500 | 0.97s | 0.73s | **1.3x** |

Note: catboost was already quite fast. Most time is spent in JSON parsing (saving model to JSON file, then reading it), which is unavoidable.

---

### cubist

**Issue: Repeated data frame subsetting with `==` in nested loops**

The original code used `coefs[coefs$rule == .x & coefs$committee == comm, ]` inside nested loops, causing O(n) scans for every rule in every committee. With 100 committees and many rules, this became O(n * committees * rules_per_committee).

**Fix:** Pre-split data frames by committee and rule using `split()` once, then use direct hash lookup by key.

| Configuration | Before | After | Speedup |
|---------------|--------|-------|---------|
| committees=10 | 0.16s | 0.15s | **1.1x** |
| committees=25 | 0.42s | 0.35s | **1.2x** |
| committees=50 | 1.09s | 0.74s | **1.5x** |
| committees=100| 2.78s | 1.64s | **1.7x** |

The speedup scales with model complexity - larger models see more benefit.

---

### rpart

Already fast - no optimization needed. <10ms for 617 nodes.

---

### partykit

**Issue: Repeated tree traversal via `nodeapply()` and `model[[.x]]`**

The original code called `partykit::nodeapply(model, .x)` and `model[[.x]]` for every single node. Each call traverses the entire tree to find that node, resulting in O(n²) complexity. 73.7% of time was spent in `rid`/`nodeids.partynode` (partykit's internal recursive tree traversal).

**Fix:** Extract all nodes at once using `partykit::nodeapply(model, ids = all_node_ids, FUN = identity)` and compute predictions using `tapply()` instead of per-node iteration.

| Configuration | Before | After | Speedup |
|---------------|--------|-------|---------|
| maxdepth=5 (61 nodes) | 0.162s | 0.005s | **32x** |
| maxdepth=10 (193 nodes) | 1.197s | 0.021s | **57x** |
| maxdepth=15 (197 nodes) | 1.212s | 0.005s | **242x** |

The speedup is dramatic because we eliminated O(n²) tree traversals.

---

### lm, glm, glmnet, earth

All regression-based models are already fast - no optimization needed.

| Model | Time | Size |
|-------|------|------|
| lm | 0.016s | 74 coefficients |
| glm | 0.012s | 74 coefficients |
| glmnet | 0.003s | 51 non-zero coefficients |
| earth | 0.065s | 41 terms |

These models are simple coefficient-based formulas with minimal computation required.

---

## Summary

All 11 model types have been profiled. Optimizations were made to 7 models:

| Model | Before | After | Speedup | Key Fix |
|-------|--------|-------|---------|---------|
| **ranger** | 10.72s | 0.92s | **11.7x** | Pre-extract columns, direct integer indexing |
| **randomForest** | 5.80s | 3.42s | **1.7x** | Pre-extract matrix columns with `unname()` |
| **lightgbm** | 5.75s | 3.71s | **1.5x** | Avoid duplicate JSON parsing, pre-extract columns |
| **catboost** | 0.97s | 0.73s | **1.3x** | Pre-extract split info once per tree |
| **cubist** | 2.78s | 1.64s | **1.7x** | Pre-split data frames by committee/rule |
| **partykit** | 1.20s | 0.02s | **57x** | Extract all nodes at once, eliminate O(n²) traversals |
| **rpart** | - | <0.01s | N/A | Already fast |
| **lm/glm/glmnet/earth** | - | <0.07s | N/A | Already fast |

**Common optimization patterns:**
1. Pre-extract data frame/matrix columns as vectors before recursive functions
2. Use direct integer indexing instead of named lookups with `as.character()`
3. Avoid repeated O(n) scans in loops - pre-split or build lookup tables
4. Avoid calling tree-traversal functions (like `nodeapply`) per-node

title: Nested case when
description:
In reference to https://github.com/tidymodels/orbital/issues/109

This PR switches all tree-based models to generate **nested `case_when()` expressions** instead of flat ones. Nested expressions mirror the tree structure, producing more efficient R and SQL code.

**Before (flat):**
```r
case_when(
  x <= 5 & y <= 3 ~ "low",
  x <= 5 & y > 3  ~ "med",
  x > 5           ~ "high"
)
```

**After (nested):**
```r
case_when(
  x <= 5 ~ case_when(
    y <= 3 ~ "low",
    .default = "med"
  ),
  .default = "high"
)
```

### Changes

#### New features
- All tree models (rpart, partykit, ranger, randomForest, xgboost, lightgbm, catboost) now generate nested `case_when()` expressions
- New vignette (`vignettes/tree-internals.Rmd`) explaining the nested approach and tree algorithms
- `parse_model()` documentation now explains the version system (v1/v2/v3) and model type classes

#### Internal improvements
- Reorganized model files with clear section headers separating nested builders from legacy code
- Extracted shared helpers to reduce duplication:
  - `apply_xgb_objective()` and `apply_lgb_objective()` for objective transformations
  - `apply_lgb_multiclass_transformation()` and `apply_catboost_multiclass_transformation()` for multiclass handling
- Documented operator naming conventions in `tree-nested.R`
- Legacy flat `case_when()` builders preserved for backwards compatibility with parsed models saved using v1/v2 format

title: add support forr DART booster in xgboost
description:
To close #183 

# Fix DART booster predictions when rate_drop > 0 (#183)

## Summary

- Fixes incorrect predictions for xgboost DART booster models when `rate_drop > 0`
- DART normalizes tree outputs using `weight_drop` values during training, which are now properly extracted and applied to each tree's predictions
- Refactors `.extract_xgb_trees()` to eliminate ~40 lines of duplicated code by reusing `parse_model()`

## Details

When using DART with dropout (`rate_drop > 0`), xgboost stores per-tree weights in `weight_drop` that must be applied during prediction. Previously, tidypredict summed tree outputs directly without these weights, causing prediction differences of ~0.11 from native `predict()`.

The fix:
1. Extracts `weight_drop` from model JSON via new `get_xgb_json_params()` helper
2. Applies weights via new `apply_dart_weights()` helper (used by both `build_fit_formula_xgb()` and `.extract_xgb_trees()`)
3. Refactors `.extract_xgb_trees()` to call `parse_model()` instead of duplicating its logic

## Test plan

- [x] DART with `rate_drop = 0` predictions match native predict
- [x] DART with `rate_drop > 0` predictions match native predict
- [x] DART `weight_drop` is extracted correctly
- [x] gbtree booster has no `weight_drop`
- [x] `.extract_xgb_trees()` combined results match `tidypredict_fit()` for DART
- [x] All existing tests pass (649 total)

title: Use `seq2()` to correctly compute indices
description:
There was a small bug in `get_xgb_path()` related to indexing that has been revealed by the dev purrr revdeps. purrr now recycles using the slightly more strict tidyverse recycling rules, and that has surfaced the issue.

To reproduce the original problem I saw, install dev purrr and run the tests, you should see something like this:

```r
> parse_model(xgb_bin_fit)
Error in `purrr::map()` at tidypredict/R/model-xgboost.R:73:2:
ℹ In index: 43.
Caused by error in `map()` at tidypredict/R/model-xgboost.R:39:2:
ℹ In index: 1.
Caused by error in `purrr::map2()` at tidypredict/R/model-xgboost.R:13:2:
! Can't recycle `.x` (size 0) to match `.y` (size 2).
```

This appeared due to some unfortunate behavior with `:` which can be fixed by switching to `seq2()` from rlang. This mimics what happens when `path` is length 1 in the original code I changed in this PR.

``` r
path <- "foo" # length 1

1:length(path) - 1
#> [1] 0
path[1:length(path) - 1]
#> character(0)

2:length(path)
#> [1] 2 1
path[2:length(path)]
#> [1] NA    "foo"
```

If possible, it would be great if we could get this fixed and sent to CRAN ahead of purrr, as it would make the purrr release a little easier. I think the purrr release is probably still at least 2 weeks out.

library(MASS)

The change to `R/acceptable.R` just removes the check for `factor`.  It turns out that `parse_model_lm` runs fine with no changes. The change to `R/te-formulas.R` strips the `factor()` from variable names when constructing the output expression.
